item.title: F-35, Bern and USA: no fixed price agreed
item.description: Report of the Supervisory Commission denies Amherd: there was no agreement on a fixed price with the US. Additional credit of CHF 394 million and reduction to 30 fighters.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Oversight Commission of the National Council: no fixed price agreed with the USA for the F-35A - Switzerland will have 30 fighter jets instead of 36; additional credit of 394 million CHF - Report criticizes lack of negotiating mandate and double-check principle - Amherd and Savic left their positions in spring 2025
## Key facts - **What**: Report by the National Council Management Commission refutes Amherd's thesis on fixed price for F-35A - When: Tuesday (date from Commission statement) - Where: Swiss Confederation, negotiations with the United States - Who: Management Commission of the National Council, Viola Amherd (former Defense Minister), Darko Savic (former Air2030 project manager) - Amount: Additional credit of 394 million CHF; additional costs estimated between 650 million and 1.3 billion CHF - Fighter jet reduction: From 36 to approximately 30 F-35A
The Management Commission of the National Council published on Tuesday a 95-page report that categorically refutes Viola Amherd's thesis: no fixed price had ever been agreed with the United States for the purchase of F-35A fighter jets. This is not merely an administrative dispute, but a matter involving the management of billions of francs in public funds and the credibility of federal institutions.
According to the Commission's statement, the Federal Defense Department and the Federal Council 'should not have assumed that a flat fixed price had been agreed upon'. The price, moreover, is not only inapplicable, but was never the subject of a contractual agreement, despite a note suggesting otherwise. The Commission cannot even 'understand the reason why the Defense Department defended this price with such firmness before Parliament'.
### Inadequate management of negotiations
The criticism does not stop at the price. The report denounces insufficiently tight organization of negotiations and inadequate flow of information. Particularly problematic is the absence, before the start of negotiations, of a clearly defined negotiating mandate. The discussions were followed by too narrow a circle of people, and in some phases 'the most elementary form of supervision' was even lacking, that is, the principle of double-check.
In 2020, the Swiss people had approved a maximum allocation of six billion francs for the purchase of 36 F-35A. Five years later, in 2025, it emerged that the price considered fixed by Bern was not guaranteed by the United States. At the end of June the previous year, the Confederation estimated additional costs between 650 million and 1.3 billion francs. Faced with this discovery, the Federal Council decided to reduce the number of fighter jets from 36 to approximately 30. To cover part of the additional costs, an additional credit of 394 million francs is still necessary.
The figure of Viola Amherd, then Defense Minister, is at the center of the investigation. Amherd had defended the thesis that the price of F-35A was fixed. Also in the spotlight is Darko Savic, former manager of the Air2030 project. Both left their respective positions in spring 2025, before the extent of the additional costs became clear. ### The timeline of a managerial error
The F-35 fighter jet case is an emblematic example of how a federal decision, initially supported by the people, can be managed defectively. In 2020, the Swiss approved an allocation of 6 billion francs based on the premise that the price was fixed and locked. This premise proved false. Five years later, hidden costs in the billions emerge, and the number of fighter jets drops from 36 to approximately 30 units.
The Supervisory Commission remains surprised by the fact that the Federal Department of Defense was able to maintain and spread, before Parliament itself, an incorrect thesis with such firmness. How was this possible? The answers lie in the management of negotiations: lack of a clearly defined negotiating mandate, fragmented communications, absence of the most basic cross-check (double control), and too narrow a circle of people involved in the decisions.
### The role of the Commission and personal responsibilities
This report represents the result of the work of the National Council's oversight. The Management Commission exercises a fundamental role: to supervise the work of the Federal Administration, to verify that the promises made to citizen-voters are kept, and to ensure the correct use of public funds. In the case of the F-35, the Commission had to dig deep to discover how the Confederation could have based a popular vote on a contractual premise that did not exist.
The additional credit of 394 million francs that is now needed to cover part of the supplementary costs comes from federal coffers. The 650-1,300 million francs of extra costs represent public resources that will not be able to be allocated to other budget chapters: health, research, infrastructure, or transport.
The individual responsibilities of Viola Amherd and Darko Savic remain at the center of the investigation. Both left their positions in the spring of 2025, well before the full extent of the problem emerged publicly. The report examines in detail the role of each in the management of negotiations and in communication to the federal leadership.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What This Decision Means for Switzerland
The acquisition of 30 F-35A instead of 36 modifies Switzerland's defensive capacity for decades to come. This is not a decision to be taken lightly, and the fact that it emerged from a critical report by the Oversight Commission suggests that the path to this reduction was anything but straightforward. The message that emerges is twofold: on one hand, the Federal Council had to downsize a failing project; on the other, the additional cost of 394 million francs still represents a draw from the federal budget. The voting citizens had subscribed to 6 billion francs for 36 fighter jets based on a premise that proved to be incorrect.
### Parliamentary Oversight as a Safeguard
The investigation by the Oversight Commission demonstrates how the Swiss Parliament, through its control bodies, is able to dig into the errors of the Federal Administration and force a correction. However, the fact that the report was necessary also indicates that internal verification systems — such as the principle of dual control recalled in the report — did not function during the negotiations. Parliamentary oversight represents an essential safeguard against errors in the management of large-scale projects with significant costs.
The Management Commission of the National Council will continue to follow the project's development. The new number of F-35A (approximately 30) and the additional credit of 394 million will have to go through ordinary parliamentary procedures, thus guaranteeing a further level of democratic control.
### Next Steps and Transparency
The 95-page report represents an opportunity for federal institutions to reflect on the governance of large defense projects and on how to manage international negotiations. The questions raised — why was a clear negotiating mandate absent? How come the flow of information was inadequate? Why was dual control lacking? — remain in principle valid for any major public purchase, regardless of sector.
The Confederation's credibility also depends on the ability to learn from these errors. Swiss citizens have the right to know how their money is managed, and transparency must remain the rule, not the exception. ## In a nutshell - Nestlé monitors AI access to its websites on a daily basis - CFO Anna Manz revealed the strategy during a conference in Boston on Tuesday - The company analyzes consumer prompts aimed at artificial intelligence - The goal is to be cited as a source by language models
## Key facts - **What**: Nestlé adapts marketing to the growing role of artificial intelligence - When: Tuesday during an investor conference - Where: Boston (conference); Vevey (Nestlé headquarters) - Who: Anna Manz, Group Finance Director - Monitoring: Daily access to language models - Heritage: 160 years of history and multi-year research activities - Strategy: Making business data accessible to language models
On Tuesday, Anna Manz, Nestlé's chief financial officer, revealed a changing business strategy at an investor conference in Boston. The group monitors on a daily basis how language models access its websites. “We monitor every day to what extent big language models interrogate our websites instead of people, and this is increasing day by day,” Manz said. This monitoring is not a niche activity, but a central operational priority. The numbers speak for themselves: AI bot access is constantly growing, transforming traffic to corporate sites.
Nestlé goes beyond simple monitoring. The company examines ## AI as the New Product Discovery Filter
Nestlé's move illuminates a broader economic trend: artificial intelligence is becoming the primary filter through which consumers discover information and products. It is not merely a technological change, but a reallocation of visibility power. When a consumer asked Google for 'best protein snack', the results were organized according to ranking algorithms. When the same consumer asks ChatGPT the same question, they receive a narrative response generated by the model. If Nestlé is not mentioned in that response, its invisibility is total. If it is recognized as a source, the effect is even more powerful than a simple ranking, because authority is attributed to it.
This explains why the daily monitoring that Manz describes is not a matter of corporate vanity, but of calculated business strategy. The company has understood that control over its own narrative in AI results has become as critical as control over its homepage. The growth of AI bot access to Nestlé's sites, described as constant and daily, testifies to the acceleration of this phenomenon. It is not temporary; it is structural.
For [Swiss companies operating in marketing, communication, and brand management](nav:companies), the message is implicit. Ignoring the phenomenon means risking becoming invisible in AI-generated results, regardless of product quality or company history. Nestlé, with its accumulated heritage advantage, is well positioned to capitalize on this transition. Smaller companies that do not adopt similar strategies risk falling behind.
### Heritage and Accessibility: The Competitive Formula
What Manz describes as an advantage — 160 years of history and years of research — is not rhetoric, but a concrete quantifiable resource. Language models are trained on vast corpora of public texts. If Nestlé makes its research data, certifications, scientific studies, and documentation easily accessible (through technical structures such as sitemaps, rich metadata, APIs), the probability of being cited as a source by models increases measurably.
It is an evolved form of SEO, applied not to traditional search engines, but to generative artificial intelligence. And the phenomenon is not a niche. Millions of people ask questions daily to chatbots; visibility in AI responses represents an unprecedented brand awareness multiplier in the era of communication.

For those working in marketing, communication and brand management in Switzerland, Nestlé's message is imperative: adaptation to AI is not optional, it is urgent. A website that is well optimized for Google is not enough; you need to ensure that your information assets are accessible and citable by current and future language models.
Concretely, the first step is to identify relevant product or service categories and analyze how consumers ask AI questions about these topics. Nestlé works with external partners to do this; smaller companies can start by directly testing public chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude and others). The critical question is simple: when a consumer asks a language model for a recommendation in your industry, is your company mentioned? If not, the next step is to understand why.
The second step is to structure the business data so that bots can access and understand it. This means:
- Publish studies, white papers and research in an open and easily citable format - Structure website metadata (schema.org, Open Graph, JSON-LD) for bots to understand context - Monitor traffic coming from language models, exactly as Nestlé does on a daily basis - Collaborate with AI and advanced SEO experts to optimize visibility into the results generated by the models

item.description: Federal and cantonal requirements to obtain residence permit C in Canton Uri: 10 years of residence, integration and language skills.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Settlement permit C normally requires 10 years of stable residence - EU/EFTA citizens: reduced threshold of 5 years - Integration and language: specific cantonal criteria - SEM manages procedure; Uri evaluates complementary criteria
## Key facts - **What**: Settlement permit (C) for stable residence - Who: Non-European foreign citizens and EU/EFTA citizens - Where: Uri Canton, central Switzerland - When: After a period of continuous legal residence - Duration: 10 years renewable - Federal Authority: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) - Fundamental criterion: Integration into the social and economic fabric
The settlement permit C represents the most stable level of legal residence in Switzerland for foreign citizens. Unlike the residence permit B (renewable annually), permit C guarantees long-term stay and represents the first step towards access to ordinary naturalization. In Uri Canton, as in all other Swiss cantons, issuance is governed by federal norms integrated with supplementary cantonal requirements.
### Federal requirements for permit C
Federal legislation sets uniform criteria at the national level. For a non-European foreign citizen, the main requirement is uninterrupted residence of 10 years on Swiss territory. This period serves to demonstrate a stable connection with the country and a verifiable capacity for integration. For citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA — Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway), the threshold is reduced to 5 years of continuous residence. This differentiation reflects bilateral free movement agreements between Switzerland and the EU.
Residence must be legal and documented. Simple physical presence does not count: a valid residence permit B is required for the entire period. During these years, the foreigner must support themselves economically through regular employment, avoid criminal convictions and respect public order. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) formally verifies these prerequisites at the federal level.
### The specific role of Uri Canton
Although SEM approves the request from a national administrative perspective, Uri Canton plays a crucial complementary role. Swiss cantons have primary authority to assess the integration of the foreigner in the local context. In the case of Uri, the cantonal administration examines criteria such as knowledge of the local language (Swiss German), participation in economic and social life, absence of conflicts with the community, stability of housing and employment situation. These criteria are not fixed: they vary slightly among cantons and may include attendance at integration or language courses, demonstration of stable relationships on the territory, certification of lasting housing situation.
For EU/EFTA citizens, the channel is slightly differentiated. Uri Canton may have less stringent rules on linguistic integration compared to third-country citizens, but control remains on the solidity of the economic situation and the absence of risks of recourse to social services. ### Differences between categories of applicants
Not all foreigners go through the same procedure for permit C. The most relevant distinction is between EU/EFTA citizens and third-country nationals. For a European Union citizen working in Uri for 5 consecutive years, an application to the SEM can be submitted earlier than for an Argentine or Chinese citizen, who must wait 10 years. In practice, this means that a European worker in the manufacturing sector or services in the Uri valley could move to permit C around the sixth year of residence, while a non-European colleague must extend their stay on permit B until the tenth year.
This differentiation is not arbitrary: the EU-Switzerland free movement agreements (2002) explicitly provide for equal treatment between Swiss and European citizens, so reducing the waiting period is a consequence of this logic. At the same time, integration remains a criterion: even at 5 years, the Canton of Uri will assess whether the applicant speaks German at a sufficient level, whether they have solid economic roots, and whether they do not present risks of marginalization.
### Integration criteria: what it means in practice
Integration is a broad term. In the context of permit C at the cantonal level, there is no single written definition: it depends on the assessment of the cantonal commission responsible. However, certain elements recur in all Swiss cantons, including Uri. First of all, knowledge of the canton's language (Swiss German and standard German) is almost always decisive. Many cantons, including Uri, require obtaining a German language proficiency certification (typically level A2 or B1 of the European framework) or in any case a positive assessment during the interview. In some cases, certified integration courses can substitute for or complement the language exam.
Second, the employment situation: the applicant must demonstrate that they exercise regular gainful activity, that they are able to support themselves, and that they do not represent a burden on public social assistance. Employment contracts, pay slips, tax returns are elements that will be examined. A long history of unemployment or dependency on social benefits can complicate the procedure. Third, residential stability: a temporary rental is not sufficient; the canton wants to know that the person has a stable home, preferably not precarious, with a long-term lease. Finally, respect for legality: no significant criminal convictions, no unpaid debts with tax authorities, no incidents of public order disturbance.
### Scenarios: who obtains permit C more easily
A European executive professional with a permanent employment contract at a construction company in Uri, who has lived in his own home or a rented one for 5 years, who speaks German fluently and has never had conflicts with the law: most likely, they will move to permit C at the end of the fifth year, perhaps in the sixth after the cantonal interview. A non-European seasonal worker who only works for 6-8 months a year for a decade, even if they have no violations, will instead have to wait all 10 years and could be required to attend language courses or specific training before approval. This does not mean discrimination: it reflects the criterion that stable integration requires continuous economic and social rootedness.

Phase 1: Preliminary legal residence (5-10 years)
Prior to any C permit application, the alien must legally reside in Uri with a valid B permit. This period is decisive. The meter starts from the first day of registration with the cantonal authority. It is not enough to live physically: you must be in possession of a continuously renewed residence permit. During these years, the person must establish and consolidate their situation: long-term employment contract, stable accommodation, possibly forming a family, social integration.
**Phase 2: Collection of documentation**
Approximately 3-6 months before the expected date of eligibility, it is advisable to start collecting the documentation. This includes: employment certificates, last 2-3 years of tax returns and pay slips, confirmation of the absence of debts to the cantonal and municipal tax authorities, certificate of good criminal conduct (to be requested from the police office of the Canton of Uri), proof of compulsory active health insurance (LAMal) without outstanding, copy of the lease or title of ownership of the property, possibly linguistic certificate (A2 or B1). ## In a nutshell - Adult deductibles: CHF 300–2500 per year, personal choice - Models: basic, HMO, network, telemedicine with different costs - Reduction: cantonal subsidy for low incomes - Obligation: registration within 3 months of residence in Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Compulsory health insurance (LAMal) in Canton Uri - When: Registration within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland - Deductibles: CHF 300/500/1000/1500/2000/2500 (adults' choice) - Models: Basic, HMO, Network, Telemedicine - Reduction: Cantonal subsidy, income-employee - Type: Private insurance per capita, no payroll tax
In Canton Uri, compulsory health insurance (LAMal) represents one of the most significant recurring expenses for those residing in Switzerland. Unlike direct federal tax or [contributi previdenziali (AVS/LPP)](nav:pension), LAMal premiums are not a wage tax, but a private collection, calculated per capita and modulated by personal choice of deductible and insurance model.
Every resident of Switzerland is required to take out health insurance within 3 months of arrival. In the Uri Canton, as in all cantons, the premiums vary according to three essential parameters: the age group, the choice of deductible, and the coverage model. Currently, the allowable deductibles for adults are CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 or 2500 per year — a choice that directly affects the amount of the monthly premium.
### Available insurance models and coverages
In the Uri Canton, as in the ## Reduction of premiums: the cantonal subsidy
The reduction of LAMal premiums in the Uri Canton takes place through the * * cantonal subsidy * *, a redistribution tool that lowers the tax burden on low- or lower-middle-income households. Unlike social security contributions (AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% for the employee), the LAMal subsidy is not automatic: those who are eligible must submit a formal application to the competent cantonal office, attaching tax documentation.
## # Grant Access Criteria
The allowance is calculated based on the household's gross annual income and the number of dependants. Each canton sets its own access thresholds and coverage percentages. In Canton Uri, as in all cantons, the subsidy covers a percentage of the premium (frequently from 20% to 100%, depending on family income), drastically reducing the monthly burden.
An illustrative practical scenario: a worker with an annual income of CHF 60,000 and two dependent children could be entitled to a subsidy that reduces the monthly premium by CHF 150–200, a substantial difference on an annual basis (CHF 1,800-2,400 per year). For those wishing to access premium reduction in Canton Uri, the procedure follows standardized steps and precise deadlines. First, it is necessary to verify whether you meet the cantonal income criteria by contacting the competent administration office or consulting the official cantonal portal.
### Step-by-step: reduction application
1. **Gather documentation**: income tax return (last 2 years), salary certificates, family composition certificates, bank statements (if requested by the office). 2. Download the application form: the official form is available at the Uri Canton Health Service office or online on the cantonal portal. 3. Complete and submit: the typical deadline is late February or early March for the current fiscal year (verify each year with the office, as dates may vary). 4. Receive the decision: the cantonal administration processes the request within 4–6 weeks and notifies you of the approved subsidy amount. 5. Transmission to the insurer: the subsidy is paid directly to the health insurance fund or reimbursed to the applicant, depending on the cantonal method.
### Timing and critical deadlines
In Canton Uri, as in almost all cantons, the application window typically opens in January and closes between February and March. Submitting the application after the deadline risks exclusion from the benefit for the current year. For those who change residence during the year and register with the canton, there is sometimes an opportunity for an additional application within a short period (e.g., 30–60 days) after administrative registration. Always verify with the local office the applicable time windows.
### Tools for comparison and decision-making
Before choosing a health fund and deductible, it is useful to: - Use the [health insurance calculator](nav:health) to compare premium offers and simulate different deductible scenarios - Consult the Uri cantonal comparator (if available on the official cantonal portal) - Contact the competent cantonal office for specific clarifications on access criteria, amounts, and required documentation - Read the policy conditions of your chosen health fund, especially regarding additional coverage (dental, optical, homeopathy)
### The first step: registration within 3 months
Remember that the first step is to register with a health fund within 3 months of your first residence in Switzerland. If you miss the deadline, the insurance can deny retroactive coverage, exposing your household to significant financial risks. Only after registration, if the subsidy application is accepted, do the premiums decrease. Timing is crucial to not lose the right to retroactive coverage and to access the current year's subsidy.

item.title: PA30+: Federal Consultation on Agriculture
item.description: PA30+ consultation with all agri-food stakeholders. News about online voting in Neuchâtel, rare diseases and climate funds.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Council launches PA30+ for agricultural policy from 2030 - Online voting authorized in Neuchâtel until November 26, 2028 - Measures for rare diseases: legal bases and national registry - Additional funds to address heat waves and drought for forests and agriculture
## Key facts - **What**: Four decisions by the Federal Council on agriculture, digital democracy, health and environment - When: PA30+ consultation launched; November 26, 2028 (end of online voting authorization); September 27, 2026 (popular vote); March 13, 2026 (transmission of EU package) - Where: National Switzerland; Canton Neuchâtel - Who: Federal Council, Parliament, citizens, agrifood chain actors - Topics: Agricultural policy, digital voting, health, climate sustainability
### The Federal Government entrusts consultation on the future of Swiss agriculture
The Federal Council has adopted a series of strategic measures that reshape the Swiss agricultural landscape, strengthen digital democracy and address health and climate challenges. The announcement comes from the official portal of the Swiss Government (admin.ch) and concerns areas that directly affect the daily life of residents in the country.
### PA30+: consultation on agricultural policy from 2030
The Federal Council has launched the consultation on PA30+ (Agricultural Policy from 2030), a comprehensive approach involving all actors in the agrifood chain. This strategy document aims to redefine the role of Swiss agriculture in a context of climate change, food security and transformation towards sustainability. The consultation is already underway and represents a crucial moment for farmers, agrifood industries, environmental associations and consumers to express their positions. Decisions made today will shape market access, prices of domestic foodstuffs and production methods in the years to come.
### Online voting: Neuchâtel opens experimentation
Secondly, the Federal Council has authorized the use of electronic voting in the Canton of Neuchâtel until November 26, 2028. This represents a significant step towards modernizing voting systems in Switzerland. A portion of voters will be able to use online voting in the context of the popular vote on November 29 next. The authorization is limited in time and restricted to the French-speaking canton, which is preparing to experiment with this innovative form of democratic participation. Data collected during the experimentation could guide decisions by cantons wishing to adopt digital voting in the future.
### Health: legal bases and national registry for rare diseases
Third issue addressed: the Federal Council wants to improve health care for people suffering from rare diseases. To this end, it intends to create legal bases for financing care facilities and information activities, as well as to establish a national registry. These measures address a historical gap in the Swiss health system, where patients with rare diseases often struggle to access coordinated care and centralized information. The national registry will allow doctors to share clinical data and patients to find their way to specialized centers.
### Additional funds to address heat waves and drought
Finally, the Federal Council has decided to adopt additional measures to deal with periods of heat waves and drought. Additional funds will be allocated to forests and agriculture, two sectors particularly vulnerable to climate stress. At the end of October, the Federal Government will reassess the situation, a sign that the response to climate crises remains dynamic and subject to revision. Investments concern emergency irrigation, forest defense and research on resistant varieties.
### Federal votes and agreements with the European Union
On September 27, 2026, Swiss citizens will vote on two initiatives: the initiative on neutrality and the one on food. In parallel, the Federal Council transmitted to Parliament on March 13, 2026 a new package of Switzerland-EU agreements aimed at stabilizing and developing bilateral relations. These agreements address key sectors of the economy and European cooperation and represent another decision front involving Parliament and, potentially, the Swiss people. ### Practical implications for the daily life of Swiss residents
The decisions of the Federal Council are not simple palace announcements: they have concrete and measurable impacts on the daily life of those who live and work in Switzerland. Let's examine how each measure affects personal finances, access to services, and opportunities for democratic participation.
### Agriculture, food prices and consumer budgets
The consultation on PA30+ concerns not only professional farmers, but anyone who buys food in supermarkets or from local producers. A reform of agricultural policy that involves 'all actors in the agrifood chain' means that prices, availability and characteristics of domestic products may vary in the coming years. If the Government decides to reduce direct subsidies to agriculture, supermarket prices could rise to reflect true production costs. If instead it encourages organic or sustainable production, consumer budgets could suffer in the short term, but benefit from a more environmentally conscious supply. Discover [how the cost of living in Switzerland changes](nav:cost-of-living) to understand which federal factors affect your daily spending on food, energy and housing.
The consultation is the crucial moment in which consumer associations, agricultural unions and organized citizens can make their voice heard before the Federal Council submits legislative proposals to Parliament. The observations received shape the final text of reforms.
### Online voting: more inclusive democracy but with security questions
The authorization of electronic voting in the Canton of Neuchâtel until November 26, 2028 represents an important pilot test for all of Switzerland. Online voting reduces physical barriers (elderly with limited mobility, people with disabilities, workers with rigid schedules) and potentially increases participation rates. However, it also raises critical questions about cybersecurity, vote traceability and voter privacy rights. The pilot in the November 29 ballot will allow the canton to gather concrete data on technical feasibility, voter acceptance and any problems encountered. This data will directly influence the decisions of other cantons regarding future extensions of digital voting.
### Rare diseases: centrality of the national registry and access to care
The national registry for rare diseases will change how patients and doctors access specialized information. Currently, those suffering from a rare disease risk wandering between hospitals without clear diagnosis or coordinated therapies, causing diagnostic delays that can last years. A centralized registry enables treating physicians to quickly connect with recognized specialists, monitor disease progression across larger samples for clinical studies, and allows patients to know where to find specialized care. The legal bases that the Federal Council intends to create will define who funds specialized structures (cantons, [LAMal/health insurance](nav:health), Confederation) and how data will flow into the registry while respecting data protection. This information is relevant to anyone who has a family member affected by a rare disease and wishes to ensure access to coordinated care and information.
### Climate and agriculture: long-term investment
Supplementary funds for forests and agriculture during periods of heat waves and drought directly address the measurable impact of climate change. Swiss farmers have suffered significant losses in recent years (2022-2023 drought, repeated heat waves). Swiss forests too, critical infrastructure for landslide prevention, water cycle and CO₂ absorption, are under increasing stress. Supplementary investments in emergency irrigation systems, forest phytosanitary defense and research on drought-resistant varieties have an evident economic return (protection of agricultural income) and environmental benefit (ecosystem preservation). The review of the situation at the end of October allows the Federal Government to adapt measures based on actual meteorological and hydrological data.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Participate: Deadlines, Procedures and Practical Tools
Federal Council decisions are not final: many steps require public consultations, parliamentary votes and popular votes. Here's what Swiss residents can concretely do in the coming months to inform themselves and participate in decision-making processes.
### Calendar of Critical Deadlines
**September 27, 2026**: First appointment with no extension. Swiss citizens will vote on two initiatives: one on neutrality and one on food. Consulting the official federal government dossiers to understand the pros and cons of each initiative is essential before voting. It's advisable to inform yourself at least a week before the vote by reading the official materials from the Federal Council on admin.ch.
November 29, 2026: In the Canton of Neuchâtel, some voters will be able to try online voting. If you reside in Neuchâtel and are eligible to vote, check with your municipal office to see if you are included in the pilot group. The pilot involves a limited number of voters, so access is not automatic.
November 26, 2028: Final deadline for authorization of online voting in Neuchâtel. Before this date, the federal government and the canton will evaluate the results of the pilot and decide whether to extend e-voting to other cantons or extend the authorization in the canton of Neuchâtel.
### Consultation on PA30+: How to Participate
The PA30+ consultation is open. If you are a farmer, agribusiness operator, environmentalist, or simply a citizen interested in Swiss agricultural policy, you can contribute by sending comments and proposals to the Federal Council within the deadlines published on admin.ch. Sector associations (Swiss Farmers' Union, small producers' associations), trade unions (Unia, VSA), and environmental organizations (Pro Natura, WWF Switzerland) are already preparing their official opinions. Informing yourself through the websites of these organizations allows you to understand the key positions at stake and formulate informed comments.
### Switzerland-EU Package: Parliamentary Monitoring
The Switzerland-EU agreement package transmitted to Parliament on March 13, 2026 now follows the standard legislative process. Parliamentary committees (economic committees, foreign affairs committees) will examine the details of the agreements in the coming months. If you are interested, the federal Parliament website (parlament.ch) allows you to follow debates in real time, consult the texts of bills and contact your representatives (national councillors and senators) to express your positions.
### Rare Diseases: How to Prepare for the National Register
If someone in your family suffers from a rare disease, following the developments of the national register is important. As soon as the legal bases are approved by Parliament and the Confederation, the register will become operational. Inform yourself through patient associations that represent your specific condition: they will be among the first to communicate the registration procedures and the practical benefits of joining the register (access to coordinated care, participation in clinical studies, connecting with other patients).
### Stay Updated and Act Consciously
The admin.ch portal remains the official source for all federal government announcements, consultation dossiers, voting calendars and legislative texts. Regularly visit the site to access details on every issue and download consultation documents. For those who want to stay updated on federal decisions, laws and reforms that affect daily life (salaries, taxes, AVS, health insurance premiums, agriculture, energy), regularly checking official communications is essential. The Frontaliere Ticino newsletter offers a weekly summary of all federal and cantonal updates relevant to Swiss residents. item.description: Complete guide to opening a business in Appenzello Interno: registration, minimum capital and AVS, LPP, LAMal obligations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Registration with the commercial register is mandatory for every business - Three legal forms: sole proprietorship, general partnership, joint-stock company - Federal social security obligations: AVS (5.3% employee), LPP (7–18% depending on age), LAINF (0.7–1.5%) - Health insurance LAMal within 3 months from the start of business activity
## Key facts - **What**: Opening a commercial business - Where: Canton Appenzell Innerrhoden - Competence: Cantonal commercial register + Federal administration (AVS/LPP/LAINF) - Tax levels: 3 (federal, cantonal, municipal) - LAMal deadline: Within 3 months from the start of business activity
Anyone starting a commercial business in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden faces a regulatory framework structured on three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. The procedure for registering with the commercial register, the obligation to subscribe to certain social insurances, and the various startup taxes represent the fundamental steps to operate regularly in Switzerland.
Registration with the commercial register is the first mandatory step. Each canton manages its own register at a specific office, where the type of legal form (sole proprietorship, general partnership, joint-stock company) and the essential company data are formalized. The minimum capital required varies depending on the chosen form: for a sole proprietorship it may be lower, while a joint-stock company has specific thresholds defined by the Federal Code of Obligations. Appenzell Innerrhoden, like all Swiss cantons, applies this federal regulation and adds its own cantonal rules for costs and procedures. It is essential to contact the cantonal Commercial Register Office directly to learn the exact amounts and necessary documents.
In parallel with registration, anyone opening a business has the obligation to fulfill various insurance obligations at the federal level. These include registration with AVS/AI, occupational pension provision through LPP, accident insurance (LAINF) if the employee reaches a minimum salary threshold, and mandatory health insurance (LAMal). These aspects do not vary by canton: they are regulated by federal law and constitute uniform obligations throughout Switzerland.
### Opening costs Opening costs include registration fees for the commercial register (specific cantonal amount), minimum capital paid (varies depending on legal form), federal insurance contributions (AVS, LPP, LAINF), and LAMal premiums (private, per capita, not a tax or contribution). Timing is critical: registration with the commercial register must take place within a specific period defined by the canton (usually a few weeks from the start of operations), while health insurance LAMal must be taken out within three months from the start of business activity, otherwise there is a risk of official registration which entails additional costs. ### Federal Insurance Obligations: Non-Negotiable Expenses
When you start a business in Switzerland, the framework of insurance obligations is defined at the federal level and applies everywhere, including Inner Appenzell. It's not a matter of choice: these are constraints governed by federal law on benefits and insurance.
#### AVS/AI (Old-Age and Disability Insurance) Anyone starting a business is required to contribute to the AVS from the beginning. If you have employees, the contribution is shared: the employee pays 5.3% of gross salary, while the employer adds another 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. It's not a negotiable percentage: it's fixed by federal law. If you work as a sole proprietor (individual business), AVS contributions vary according to declared net income, but are mandatory nonetheless.
#### AD/AC (Unemployment Insurance) Alongside the AVS, employees and employers also contribute to the AD: 1.1% of salary up to an annual maximum. This covers the risk of unemployment. Like the AVS, it's a mandatory and non-negotiable deduction.
#### LAINF/LAA (Accident Insurance) If your employee reaches a minimum annual salary threshold, you are required to insure them against accidents. The contribution ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% of coordinated salary, depending on the sector. A craft business has a different contribution rate than an office or industrial business. SUVA is the main entity, but other insurers exist. Costs depend on the risk profile of your business.
#### LPP/BVG (Occupational Pension Law) Occupational pensions are mandatory for employees earning above a certain threshold (coordination). The contribution depends on the employee's age and is shared between employee and employer. For employees aged 25–34 the contribution is 7%, 35–44 years 10%, 45–54 years 15%, 55 years until retirement age (normally 65) 18%. These rates apply to coordinated salary (gross salary minus a federal deduction, indexed annually). It's the main pension cost after the AVS.
#### LAMal/KVG (Mandatory Health Insurance) Every resident in Switzerland is obliged to take out health insurance within three months of starting a business (or upon arrival in Switzerland if foreign). It's not a tax, but a private subscription with a per capita premium. Premiums vary by canton, region, and insurance company, and depend on age bracket and chosen deductible. Standard deductibles for adults start at CHF 300 annually up to CHF 2500. Inner Appenzell, like every canton, offers cantonal subsidies for premiums to people with low incomes. The deadline is critical: if you don't subscribe within three months, the canton proceeds with automatic enrollment (tacit registration) with potentially higher premiums and retroactive effect.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Practical Checklist for Opening a Business in Appenzell Innerrhoden
Following a logical order reduces the risk of errors and penalties. Here are the concrete steps to start your business properly.
#### Step 1: Choose the Legal Structure and Verify Minimum Capital Contact the Commercial Register Office of Appenzell Innerrhoden for advice on sole proprietorship, partnership, or limited company. Each form has different minimum capital requirements and obligations. Do not proceed further until you have clarified this fundamental point with the competent office.
#### Step 2: Registration in the Commercial Register Once you have the required documents (property register extract, lease contract for space, certificates, etc.), register with the cantonal office. Registration must take place within a period set by the canton (usually 30–60 days from the actual start of your business). The cost varies by canton and is set by the cantonal fees: contact the office for an exact quote.
#### Step 3: Registration with AVS/AI within 5 days Immediately after registration in the commercial register, you must register with AVS at the federal single number (the Coordinated Federal Administrations). This is a non-negotiable federal obligation. If you hire employees, the registration includes them as well: each employee must have an AVS number.
#### Step 4: Registration with Accident Insurance (LAINF/LAA) Contact a LAINF insurer (SUVA or authorized private companies) to insure your employees. Ask for the specific risk profile of your business: this determines the percentage premium (0.7%–1.5% of coordinated salary).
#### Step 5: Health Insurance (LAMal) — within 3 months Choose an insurance company from those operating in Switzerland and take out a policy [nav:health]. The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden (through the social insurance office) provides a list of authorized companies and their premium ranges. Compare prices: there are significant variations between companies even for the same canton. The minimum deductible is CHF 300 per year for adults. Remember that the deadline is non-negotiable: three months from the start of your business.
#### Step 6: Occupational Pension (LPP) for Employees If you hire employees, register them with an LPP occupational pension fund [nav:pension] before the start of their employment. Contributions begin on the first day and depend on the employee's age (7% for ages 25–34, 10% for 35–44, 15% for 45–54, 18% for 55+ up to the reference age). Each fund has its own registration rules: contact it with the employee's details.
### Critical Deadlines The commercial register must be completed within 30–60 days from the start of your business. AVS must be registered within 5 days of commercial registration. Health insurance LAMal has an absolute deadline: within 3 months from the start of your business. LAINF must begin before the start of your business if you hire employees immediately.
### Total Costs (Qualitative Estimate) Fixed opening costs include commercial register registration fee (variable by canton), minimum capital payment (variable by legal structure), first LAINF premium (varies by sector), first LAMal premium (varies by canton and owner's age), LPP registration (usually free, but with mandatory contributions from the first month).
For an exact estimate, contact the Appenzell Innerrhoden cantonal administration or the official cantonal website (www.ai.ch).
### Next Steps Once your business is open, you must submit your tax return within federal and cantonal deadlines (usually 90 days after the end of the fiscal year). AVS and LPP contributions will become a regular monthly expense, as will LAMal premiums. To calculate the tax and pension impact of operational costs on your business, use our [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: Foreign driver's license in Lucerne: conversion and exams
item.description: Complete procedure to convert international driving license in the Canton of Lucerne: requirements, theoretical and practical exam, compulsory courses and times.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Conversion of a foreign driver's license in the Canton of Lucerne requires a formal application to the traffic office. - Theoretical and practical exams are mandatory for all foreign candidates. - Instructional and guided driving courses are part of the standard procedure.
## Key facts - **What**: Conversion of an international driving licence into a Swiss licence - Where: Canton Lucerne, Cantonal Traffic Office (Straßenverkehr Office) - Who: Foreign drivers resident in the canton - Requirements: Theoretical exam, practical exam, compulsory courses at an authorized school - Documents: Passport, foreign license, certificate of residence, medical certificate if required
In the Canton of Lucerne, as in all Swiss cantons, converting an international driving licence into a Swiss licence requires you to go through a standardised procedure at the relevant traffic office. This is not an automatic conversion: it is not enough to present the foreign document, but it is necessary to prove that you know the Swiss road traffic regulations and that you are a safe driver according to Swiss standards.
### Three stages of conversion
The procedure is divided into three main phases. First of all, the candidate submits a formal application to the circulation office, accompanied by the required documents (passport or identity document, residence permit if foreign, medical certificate if necessary, and copy of the foreign license). ## New Responsibilities and Regulatory Differences
Once a Swiss driving license is obtained in Canton Lucerne, the driver assumes full responsibility according to Swiss laws. Any violations, accidents, or traffic offenses are regulated by Swiss legislation and recorded in the central Swiss driver register. Penalties include fines, license suspension, or demerit points depending on the severity of the offense.
### Validity of Foreign Driving License in Switzerland
A foreign driving license obtained from a third country (non-EU/EFTA) is recognized by Switzerland for a temporary period, usually up to 12 months from the time of settlement as a resident. After this period expires, conversion becomes mandatory. For those coming from EU/EFTA countries, recognition is longer, but conversion remains mandatory for permanent residents.
An important aspect concerns road safety courses after conversion. In Canton Lucerne, if the driver commits serious traffic offenses (driving under the influence, dangerous speeding, reckless driving) within the first 3 years of obtaining a Swiss driving license, they may be required to take a road safety awareness course before their license is recognized again.
### Costs and Timeline Planning
The total cost of conversion depends on: administrative fees for the application, number of driving lessons required, examination fees (theoretical and practical), and the cost of instruction at an authorized driving school. Overall, the candidate must plan to invest time in preparation and completion of all stages.
Local driving schools offer standardized packages and the public traffic office provides exam schedules at least a few weeks in advance. If the candidate does not pass the theoretical or practical examination on the first attempt, they must take the exam again in a subsequent session, which involves additional time and costs. Every Swiss canton follows the same federal road traffic regulatory structure, ensuring uniformity of rules throughout the national territory.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## Step-by-step procedure to start the conversion
Step 1: Gather necessary documents Before contacting the traffic office, make sure you have: valid identification document (passport or ID card), original foreign driver's license and copy, proof of residence in Canton Lucerne, medical certificate if required, and any documentation of past violations in other countries. Check with the office if other documents are necessary.
Step 2: Contact the cantonal traffic office Canton Lucerne has a central traffic office with branches in the main municipalities. Call or visit the canton's official website to book an appointment. The office will examine your application, verify the requirements, and communicate the next steps of the procedure.
Step 3: Enroll in an authorized driving school If required, choose a driving school recognized by the canton and register for mandatory courses. Schools provide packages that include theoretical lessons, practical driving, and exam preparation. Ask directly about the average course duration and total cost.
Step 4: Take the theoretical exam Once you have completed the course (or if exempted), contact the traffic office to register for the theoretical exam. The exam takes place at one of the canton's authorized exam centers and covers Swiss traffic laws. Prepare with official study materials provided by the canton or the driving school.
Step 5: Take the practical exam After passing the theoretical exam, book the practical exam with an authorized examiner. During the test, demonstrate competence in vehicle control and compliance with traffic law. If you don't pass the exam, you can retake it in the next session.
Step 6: Obtain the Swiss driver's license Once you have passed both exams, the Swiss driver's license is issued by the traffic office. The document is valid for Canton Lucerne and recognized throughout Switzerland and in many foreign countries according to reciprocal agreements.
### Indicative timelines
The entire process, from initial application to license issuance, can take 2-4 months depending on the frequency of available exams and the time needed for preparatory courses. item.title: Neutrality: Switzerland at the polls for the initiative
item.description: Oscar Freysinger calls for a vote in favour of the Neutrality Initiative. Over 300 participants at the Swiss Pro Festival in Lugano.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Over 300 people at the Pro Switzerland Neutrality Festival in Lugano - Oscar Freysinger: 'Neutrality is Switzerland's DNA, there is no semi-neutrality' - Upcoming vote on the Neutrality Initiative with voices from left to right - Request to inscribe the principle in the Swiss Constitution
## Key facts - **What**: Neutrality Festival with debate on the upcoming federal consultation - When: evening organized by Pro Switzerland (date not specified in the source) - Where: Pregassona Hall, Lugano - Who: Oscar Freysinger, Marco Chiesa (UDC), Lorenzo Quadri (Lega), Adam Barbato, and other exponents - Participants: over 300 people
### When neutrality becomes a public debate topic
Over 300 people filled the Pregassona Hall in Lugano to participate in the Neutrality Festival organized by Pro Switzerland, an event dedicated to a fundamental principle of Swiss foreign policy. The evening, moderated by Diego Baratti, brought together political figures from various backgrounds: Marco Chiesa (UDC), Maria Pia Ambrosetti (Independent), Adam Barbato (communist youth), Lorenzo Quadri (Lega), Massimiliano Ay (PC) and Paolo Pamini (UDC).
The central guest of the event was Oscar Freysinger, former UDC national councillor and former Valais State councillor. In his intervention, Freysinger retraced the history of Swiss neutrality, emphasizing the value this principle has held in international diplomacy. 'Neutrality is not just any characteristic of Switzerland, it is its DNA,' he stated during the evening.
Freysinger's statement emphasized a recurring concept in the debate on the upcoming consultation: the principle of neutrality admits no gray areas. 'Neutrality is like life: either you are alive or you are not. Similarly, there is no semi-neutrality,' Freysinger explained, adding that being neutral means 'a total commitment, not a partial one, to peace and the victims.'
According to the former national councillor, neutrality does not represent an isolation of Switzerland from the rest of the world, but rather a tool that allows it to maintain dialogue with all contenders. 'Neutrality opens all doors,' he emphasized. Freysinger then invited those present to support the Neutrality Initiative, asking that the principle be clearly inscribed in the Constitution and that the Confederation focus on independence, diplomacy and mediation to prevent and resolve conflicts.
### The perspective of a national manifestation
The presence of representatives from different political forces — from left to right — testifies to how the issue of neutrality transcends traditional ideological divisions. While starting from different perspectives, the public debate on the subject touches on issues that engage the entire Swiss political class. Freysinger concluded his speech with an explicit warning: 'Switzerland must in no way participate in this game of deceptions. And the only way to escape it is called neutrality.'
The evening then concluded with convivial and musical moments, transforming from political debate to a broader space for discussion on the direction Switzerland intends to follow in the coming years. ### Neutrality and implications for Swiss foreign policy
Swiss neutrality is not merely a historical choice, but a cornerstone that has allowed the Country to perform diplomatic and humanitarian roles recognized worldwide. According to what was emphasized by Freysinger during the event, the Confederation has been able to offer its good offices, facilitate negotiations between belligerent parties, and maintain a prominent humanitarian position in the international system, precisely thanks to this commitment to military non-alignment.
In recent years, global geopolitical tensions and ongoing conflicts have brought back to the center of Swiss public debate the question of how the Country can maintain coherence in its foreign policy principles. Freysinger highlighted that the concept of 'semi-neutrality' — that is, a selective neutrality based on geopolitical circumstances — represents a logical and political inconsistency. According to this argument, it is not possible to choose to be neutral only when it is convenient or on a case-by-case basis.
### Why an initiative on neutrality
The Initiative for Neutrality, which will be the subject of an upcoming popular consultation, proposes to anchor the principle directly in the Swiss Constitution in explicit and binding terms. Currently, neutrality is part of Swiss constitutional tradition and diplomatic practice, but it is not always formalized in the most rigid terms that the initiative proposes.
The debate that emerges from the Lugano event reflects a tension present in Swiss politics: how to balance the commitment to economic, commercial, and cultural alliances with international partners, while maintaining at the same time a position of decision-making autonomy in military and political matters. Swiss neutrality has also historically favored the stability of the Swiss franc (CHF) on the international market, allowing the Country to negotiate commercial agreements from a position of strength. Understanding Switzerland's monetary stability is relevant when considering the economic implications of a coherent foreign policy.
### The role of diplomacy and mediation
Freysinger insisted that neutrality does not entail passivity. On the contrary, Switzerland can exercise greater influence through diplomacy, mediation, and the universal recognition of its impartial position. This approach has historically allowed international organizations headquartered in Switzerland to operate in conflict contexts with access and legitimacy that a non-neutral country might not have.
The event revealed how the theme of neutrality attracts cross-party support: from communist youth to traditional right and center parties, passing through organized civil society. This broad support suggests that the upcoming consultation will touch a sensitive chord in Swiss collective sentiment.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What happens now: the national consultation
The upcoming vote on the Initiative for Neutrality will constitute a decisive moment for Switzerland. Although the source does not specify the exact date of the consultation, the demonstration in Lugano indicates that the debate is already in an active phase in the territory. Swiss citizens will have the opportunity to express themselves directly on a matter of constitutional scope.
### How to inform yourself before voting
For those wishing to deepen their understanding of the topic before the consultation, it is useful to consult the official materials of the Federal Administration, which provides explanatory documents on each popular initiative subject to a vote. It is advisable to read the full text of the initiative, the arguments for and against, and the positions of federal institutions. In-depth articles on national news sites allow you to understand the various political perspectives on the topic.
### The meaning of the vote on neutrality
A vote on neutrality is not a marginal or purely theoretical issue. The decisions that Switzerland makes in the field of foreign policy have concrete implications for commercial relations, international agreements, the tax structure and tax conventions of the Confederation, participation in supranational bodies, and potentially on the geopolitical positioning of the country in the coming decades. Every Swiss citizen who goes to the polls will contribute to defining which path the country intends to take.
The Celebration for Neutrality by Pro Switzerland testifies that this is not a debate limited to political circles, but a matter that mobilizes civil society. The over 300 people present in Lugano represent only a fraction of the population that will have to express themselves, but they signal the level of attention the topic is receiving.
### Practical steps to participate in the vote
As with every federal consultation, Swiss citizens will receive voting materials at home in the days preceding the vote. It is possible to participate in person at your own municipality or by mail. Consulting the specific deadlines at the municipal administration is the first step to ensure your participation.
Consciously participating in federal votes means also considering how these decisions impact the national economy. Choices on neutrality influence Switzerland's international commercial relations, which in turn impact employment and wage levels in the country. For those wishing to deepen these aspects and stay updated on federal economic policy issues that impact the Swiss labor market, it is possible to consult specialized resources.

item.title: Air traffic and emissions: return to pre-Covid levels
item.description: In 2025, Switzerland recorded 1.4 million air movements and 60.5 million passengers. CO2 emissions are growing (+3%). UST confirms the pre-Covid recovery.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In 2025, Swiss air traffic exceeds pre-Covid levels with 1.4 million aircraft movements - Fuel consumption grows to 1.83 million tons with CO2 emissions +3% - Air safety shows clear improvement: incidents halved in 2025
## Key facts - **What**: Statistics on air traffic and emissions in Switzerland for 2025 - When: Data released by the Federal Statistical Office - Where: Zurich, Geneva, Basel-Mulhouse airports - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Aircraft movements: 1.4 million (+5% vs 2024, +3% vs 2019) - Passengers: 60.5 million (+4% vs 2024, +2% vs 2019) - CO2 emissions: 5.74 million tons (+3% vs 2024)
In 2025, for the first time after the pandemic, air transport in Switzerland surpassed the volumes recorded before the Covid-19 crisis. The Federal Statistical Office released today the official data: Swiss civil aviation recorded 1.4 million aircraft movements (take-offs and landings), 5% more than in 2024 and 3% more than in 2019, the last pre-pandemic year. The number of passengers reached 60.5 million, with increases of 4% compared to 2024 and 2% compared to 2019. However, the recovery of aviation is accompanied by a significant increase in CO2 emissions and energy consumption.
### The three main hubs and traffic distribution
General aviation, which operates with small aircraft, represented 68% of all aircraft movements in 2025. Scheduled and charter flights, instead, dominated the passenger flow with a share of 99%. The three main Swiss airports recorded differentiated trends. Zurich marked a +4%, reaching 32.5 million passengers; Basel-Mulhouse achieved an increase of over 8%, reaching 9.6 million; Geneva, instead, remained substantially stable at 17.7 million. The total distance covered by passengers grew by over 6%, underscoring that flights were not only more numerous, but also on routes that were on average longer. The average seat load factor instead decreased from 82% to 79%, a figure that reveals how the sector had to increase supply capacity to cover heterogeneous demand, with the most significant decline recorded on routes to North America and Asia. The growth in traffic has had direct consequences on energy consumption and environmental emissions. In 2025, approximately 1.83 million tonnes of aircraft fuel were supplied in Switzerland, compared to 1.77 million tonnes in the previous year. This increase of around 60,000 tonnes generated a corresponding 3% increase in CO2 emissions, reaching 5.74 million tonnes. In parallel, emissions of nitrogen oxides (air pollutant) also increased, highlighting the overall environmental impact of the recovery in air traffic.
### The Efficiency Paradox: More Passengers, Empty Seats
A clear finding emerges from the analysis: despite the increase in the number of passengers, the average aircraft occupancy rate declined. This means that airlines operated with more aircraft and more frequencies to meet demand, but did not completely fill available seats. The drop from 82% to 79% average occupancy suggests a strategy of increasing capacity even when demand did not fully require it, or a redistribution of flights on less profitable routes with lower congestion.
This phenomenon directly impacts environmental sustainability: flights with fewer passengers per capita mean greater fuel consumption and higher emissions for each individual passenger transported. For those who fly regularly to or from Switzerland, understanding these dynamics helps evaluate personal transport choices and their impact on personal finances. Even small decisions about flight routing (direct vs. connecting, changing flight times for a less crowded time slot) can affect individual costs and the management of [payslip](nav:payslip) allocated to air travel.
### Air Safety in Marked Improvement
Contrary to the negative trend in emissions, Switzerland's air safety chapter records clear and reassuring improvement. The number of incidents and serious events involving aircraft registered in Switzerland fell from 23 in 2024 to 10 in 2025. Deaths decreased from 5 to 3, while serious injuries fell from 7 to 5. These numbers reflect increasingly rigorous technological and procedural standards in the civil aviation sector, despite the significant increase in total traffic volume.

For those who live and work in Switzerland, these data offer important insights for reflection on their own mobility and how it integrates into the national economy. Air transport is not merely a matter of vacations and personal business: it represents a strategic axis for Swiss connectivity with the rest of Europe and the world, influencing competitiveness and economic opportunities.
### How to monitor official data
The Federal Statistical Office regularly publishes detailed statistics on air transport in its dedicated transportation section. Consulting this data makes it possible to understand the trend of the economy and national competitiveness in the medium term. The Swiss airports in Zurich, Geneva, and Basel-Mulhouse represent critical infrastructure that reflects the health of the Swiss economic system and the capacity to attract international investments and talent.
### Future scenarios and cost implications
The growth of air traffic, accompanied by an increase in CO2 emissions, is not sustainable indefinitely. At the federal level, Switzerland pursues binding emission reduction targets by 2030 and climate neutrality by 2050. This means that the aviation sector will be subject to increasingly greater regulatory pressures: development of sustainable fuel (SAF), aircraft efficiency improvements, possible taxes or emission compensation systems. For the Swiss citizen, this will likely result in an increase in the cost of airfare in the medium term. Evaluating today how [cost of living and mobility](nav:cost-of-living) integrate into your personal budget becomes increasingly relevant for planning future expenses.
### Action: monitor and optimize your mobility
If you are frequent users of domestic or international flights, begin to reflect on how to optimize your travels and related expenses. Compare the transportation options available in Switzerland: railways, buses, car-sharing can represent valid alternatives depending on your route and your needs. Understanding the [Swiss transportation system](nav:transport) will help you make choices that are conscious both economically and environmentally. The Federal Statistical Office will continue to monitor the evolution of air traffic in the coming years: stay updated by regularly consulting the official data to anticipate changes in costs and flight availability for your personal and professional needs.

item.title: ABB and Rolls-Royce: Nuclear Reactors Alliance
item.description: The giant ABB together with Rolls-Royce SMR for automation solutions in small modular reactors. Generative capacity: 470 MW with low carbon emissions.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - ABB and Rolls-Royce SMR sign memorandum of understanding for nuclear reactors - Capacity: 470 MW of low-carbon electricity - Projects underway in North Wales, Czech Republic and Sweden
## Key facts - **What**: Memorandum of understanding between ABB (Switzerland) and Rolls-Royce SMR (United Kingdom) - When: Press release today - Where: North Wales, Czech Republic, Sweden - Who: ABB, Rolls-Royce SMR, ČEZ, Videberg Kraft - Capacity: 470 MW of electricity with low carbon emissions
### A strategic alliance for next-generation nuclear energy
Swiss electrical engineering giant ABB and British company Rolls-Royce SMR have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore automation and electrification solutions designed for small modular reactors. The agreement represents a strategic move to accelerate the spread of next-generation nuclear energy on a global scale.
The small modular reactors (SMRs) at the heart of the alliance are capable of generating 470 MW of low-carbon electricity, a capacity sufficient to power one million homes in the United Kingdom for 60 years.
Rolls-Royce SMR has already launched design activities for the first three plants in North Wales, which will create thousands of jobs, as ABB reports in today's press release. The British company is also active in the Czech Republic, where it collaborates with partner ČEZ at Temelín. More recently, it was selected by Videberg Kraft to build three SMRs on the Swedish peninsula of Värö.
Stacy O'Brien, senior executive at Rolls-Royce SMR, highlighted the value of the standardized approach: 'Rolls-Royce SMR is transforming the way nuclear projects are implemented, ensuring greater certainty on costs and timelines through a standardized approach and factory-built manufacturing'.
ABB, global leader in automation and electrification, will bring to this collaboration decades of experience in providing solutions for energy infrastructure. Erik Holsten, division head at ABB, reaffirmed the importance of collaboration: 'Collaboration is essential. No single company or country can alone achieve the scale of expansion and energy transformation necessary to meet future demand'. ### Implications for the global energy strategy
ABB has been operating in the industrial automation and energy sector for decades, with a consolidated presence in Switzerland and internationally. A partnership with Rolls-Royce SMR represents a strategic positioning for ABB in the emerging market for small modular reactors, which analysts consider one of the most promising solutions for the global energy transition.
Small modular reactors differ from large traditional nuclear plants in flexibility, potentially reduced construction costs and compatibility with distributed energy networks. Rolls-Royce SMR has developed a standardised, factory-built approach, elements that contribute to greater certainty in costs and lead times — critical factors that have always held back investment in nuclear energy.
ABB contributes to this partnership with its expertise in automation, process control and electrification. These elements are essential for the efficient and safe operation of nuclear plants, both small and large. The company said it took the opportunity to "further strengthen our implementation team" in this collaboration, indicating a potential increase in investments in human and technological resources.
### The prospects of the International Energy Agency
The prospects for small modular reactors are significant.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What this partnership means for the sector
The collaboration between ABB and Rolls-Royce SMR is not only a commercial partnership, but a crucial market signal: the main players in the global energy transition believe SMRs are mature for significant scale-up in the coming decades. ABB, with over a century of history in industrial automation and providing critical solutions for energy infrastructure, would not have signed this memorandum without seriously evaluating the commercial growth potential of the SMR sector.
For European governments and regulators, this news communicates a clear message: the private sector is ready to invest in small modular reactors once regulatory conditions become predictable and stable. The critical variable remains political support: reducing regulatory approval times, providing regulatory clarity on standards and licenses, and in some cases providing initial incentives or investment guarantees.
### Next steps and the role of regulation
Rolls-Royce SMR is currently in the final design stages for the first three plants in North Wales. If the projects proceed according to announced plans, they will represent the first commercial-scale test of the British company's standardized and factory-built approach. Parallel projects in the Czech Republic (Temelín with ČEZ) and Sweden (Värö with Videberg Kraft) will follow the same technical and commercial model, accumulating operational experience and building a credible track record for investors and financiers.
For those following energy infrastructure development in Europe, these projects represent a fundamental testing ground. The commercial and operational success of SMRs in the next 5-10 years will determine whether the International Energy Agency's predictions — 40 GW in the prudent scenario, up to 120 GW with political support by 2050 — are realistic or overly optimistic.
