item.title: Migros online: +21,000 products in Regensdorf
item.description: New logistics hub in Regensdorf (ZH) with 60% more products, 7,500 orders/day, 200-500 jobs. Same-day deliveries to Zurich by February 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Migros doubles online assortment: 12,500 → 21,000 products (+60%) - Hub Regensdorf handles 7,500 orders/day on 38,000 m² over 4 floors - Target 70% capacity by February 2027; 200-500 employees - Revenue CHF 362 million, 47% Swiss online market
## Key facts - **What**: New Migros Online logistics centre in Regensdorf, Zurich - When: May 2026 (phased), 70% capacity by February 2027 - Where: Regensdorf (ZH); replaces Pratteln (BL) and Bremgarten (AG) - Who: Migros, manager Katrin Tschannen - Capacity: 7,500 orders/day, 200-500 employees - Turnover: CHF 362 million (2025), market share 47% - Growth: +17% orders August vs previous year, +12% turnover
Migros accelerates online commerce with the new Regensdorf distribution center. Gradually put into operation at the end of May, the logistics hub represents the decisive step in the digital strategy of the main Swiss chain in a very competitive market: Migros Online has 47% of the national e-commerce market share, while Coop.ch holds 48%.
The assortment available on the online platform increases by 60%, from 12,500 to 21,000 products. The offer thus reaches the breadth of a traditional MMM supermarket, bridging the gap between digital catalogue and physical store. The new hub, built on approximately 38,000 square metres spread over four floors, has an operating capacity of 7,500 orders per day.
### Phase ## Economic and Employment Implications
The ramp-up of the Regensdorf center reflects a precise strategy by Migros to capitalize on e-commerce growth in Switzerland. The past two years have shown that previous logistics capacity was insufficient. In August alone, online orders increased by 17% compared to the same period of the previous year, and the division's revenue grew by 12%. Migros Online achieved annual revenue of 362 million francs last year, positioning itself in a close battle with Coop.ch for digital market leadership: 47% market share against 48% for its main competitor.
According to Katrin Tschannen, head of the division, the bet on growth is firm: the stated goal is average annual growth exceeding 10%. This means that the new center was not oversized for the present, but designed as flexible infrastructure that will support expansion in the coming years.
### Delivery Speed and Competitive Advantages
Greater logistics capacity enables significant reductions in delivery times. In the Zurich metropolitan area, within the medium term, same-day deliveries will be possible. This represents a competitive advantage in a highly densified region where orders are concentrated. Fulfillment speed is increasingly a decisive factor in consumers' choice between digital platforms, especially for fresh products.
### Managing Initial Shortfalls
The gradual launch of the facility had caused temporary gaps in the online shop, particularly for some fresh products. Migros is currently working to resolve these continuity issues. Full achievement of operational capacity by February 2027 should stabilize the offering across all product categories.
### Impact on the Swiss Labor Market
From an employment perspective, the new center represents an investment in the logistics infrastructure of German-speaking Switzerland. The relocation of 250 employees from Pratteln and Bremgarten to Regensdorf, with three-quarters of them accepting, demonstrates the company's willingness to maintain employment continuity despite logistics consolidation. The expansion to 200-500 positions in the new hub generates positive dynamics for the Zurich area, historically a hub of attraction for the Swiss supply chain and the tertiary sector labor market.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How to Follow Migros Online's Evolution
Those who want to stay updated on Migros Online's performance and growth strategies can regularly consult the chain's official communications. The main deadlines are already public: reaching 70% operational capacity by February 2027 represents a milestone that Migros has communicated publicly and which can be monitored through quarterly and annual corporate reports.
### Employment Opportunities in the Swiss Logistics Sector
The new center is emblematic of a broader trend: e-commerce growth in Switzerland is transforming the occupational landscape of logistics and distribution. Those interested in positions in the supply chain sector — from warehouse management to picking, from quality control to supervisory roles — will find in the Regensdorf project and similar Coop investments an indication of emerging opportunities in the Swiss labor market. [Discover job offers in logistics and distribution](nav:jobs)
### Impact for the Swiss Consumer
On the consumer front, Migros Online's expansion to 21,000 products (from the previous base of 12,500) means significantly increased choice. The possibility of same-day deliveries in the Zurich area makes the service more competitive compared to international pure-play online retailers. For those living or working in German-speaking Switzerland, particularly around Zurich and in the Regensdorf area, the service will become progressively more convenient and faster.
### Next Territorial Developments
The further development planned in French-speaking Switzerland (a 60,000 m² project with 400-500 employees for the basin served by Ecublens) suggests that Migros will continue to invest in territorial logistics capacity. This alignment between online demand growth and local infrastructure represents a different market choice compared to centralized European models, and signals confidence in the potential of the Swiss market in the medium to long term. item.title: Slightly falling electricity prices in 2027
item.description: In 2027, Swiss domestic economies will pay 26.5 ct./kWh average tariff: a 4% drop and savings of CHF 53 per year according to ElCom.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In 2027, average energy tariff at 26.5 ct/kWh, a 4% decline compared to 2026 - Annual bill: 1,194 francs (-53 francs), thanks to falling procurement costs - Energy tariff down 6.28%, but grid rises by approximately 2% - ElCom: 580 operators reported new tariffs by August 31, 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Falling electricity prices in the Swiss universal service - When: Effective January 1, 2027 (announcement September 8, 2026) - Where: Switzerland (households in universal service) - Who: Federal Electricity Commission (ElCom) + 580 network operators - Average tariff: 26.5 ct./kWh (decline of 1.2 ct./kWh from 2026) - Annual amount: Bill CHF 1,194 (-CHF 53 compared to 2026) - Energy tariff: Down 6.28% to 11.35 ct./kWh - Network tariff: Up from 10.73 to 10.94 ct./kWh
The Federal Electricity Commission (ElCom) announced on September 8, 2026, new tariffs for 2027. In the coming year, Swiss households will continue to benefit from falling electricity prices: the median tariff will drop to 26.5 cents per kilowatt-hour (ct./kWh), with an average decline of 4% compared to 2026. This means that a standard household with an annual consumption of 4,500 kWh will pay a bill of approximately 1,194 francs, saving 53 francs per year.
The decline is driven primarily by a reduction in energy procurement costs. The specific energy tariff (the component most directly linked to raw material prices) will fall by 6.28%, dropping from 12.11 to 11.35 ct./kWh. However, this advantage is partially offset by an increase in the network tariff, which will rise from 10.73 to 10.94 ct./kWh, and by the increase in the metering tariff, which will rise by 4 francs annually to 78.48 francs.
By August 31, 2026, approximately 580 Swiss network operators reported new tariffs for 2027 to ElCom and their customers. However, the median figures conceal a heterogeneous reality: prices vary considerably from one operator to another, primarily due to differences in procurement strategies and the share of own generation. As ElCom emphasizes, metering tariffs range between 0 and 180 francs annually, testifying to significant disparities among regional networks.
### The Iran War and Its Effect on Already Concluded Contracts
The current rise in wholesale energy market prices, due to the Iran war that broke out in March 2026, will have a limited impact on 2027 tariffs. The reason is simple: suppliers have already concluded their structured procurement contracts for 2027 before the geopolitical escalation. As ElCom notes, wholesale prices have stabilized at the usual rather high level, but the visible effects of the current conflict on the Swiss bill will appear only in the following years, when old contracts expire and are renewed at potentially higher prices. Meanwhile, many suppliers will continue to benefit from the expiration of contracts concluded at particularly high prices in previous years. The energy bill remains a significant element of the Swiss cost of living. An average family with a consumption of 4,500 kWh per year spent approximately 1,247 francs in 2026. In 2027, this amount will drop to approximately 1,194 francs, a modest cut in absolute terms but one that fits positively within a context of inflationary pressures still present in various areas of household spending.
The overall 4% decline masks contrasting internal dynamics. While the price of energy falls thanks to the easing of global supply costs, network infrastructure (management, maintenance, investments in technology) continues to weigh on bills. This phenomenon reflects a structural Swiss trend: the country is heavily dependent on the transport of energy through high and medium voltage lines managed by Swissgrid and regional operators. These infrastructure costs do not decrease proportionally to wholesale prices and, indeed, tend to grow when investments in renewables and grid digitalization (smart metering) are needed.
### Regional variability and the role of network operators
A crucial aspect highlighted by ElCom is the high variability of tariffs among the 580 Swiss network operators. The median tariff of 26.5 ct./kWh is precisely a median value, which means that half of the operators apply lower tariffs and half apply higher ones. In some cases, this dispersion is considerable: the metering tariff, for example, ranges between 0 and 180 francs per year for a household, a range that reflects very different strategic choices regarding measurement technology and service management.
These differences stem from divergent purchasing strategies. Some operators, especially in areas with strong local hydroelectric production (Alps), benefit from naturally lower supply costs. Others, in lowland areas or in cities, depend heavily on wholesale markets and inter-cantonal distribution networks. Furthermore, investment in network infrastructure varies considerably: those with recently new or renovated plants will pay higher network tariffs to amortize these costs, while those with networks consolidated for decades will have lower costs. For consumers, this means that their 2027 bill could be significantly different from the national median.
### The role of WACC and the economic balance of networks
A technical but important element concerns the rate of remuneration of capital invested in networks, the so-called WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital). In 2027 it has fallen from 3.43% to 3.28%, an apparently small reduction but one that has generated an aggregate saving of approximately 34 million francs distributed across all Swiss networks, equivalent to an average reduction of the network tariff of 0.06 ct./kWh. It is a signal that global interest rates remain under control and that the financing of energy infrastructure remains economically sustainable. At the same time, the supplementary tariff for winter reserve costs falls from 0.41 ct./kWh to 0.17 ct./kWh, partly offsetting the increase in the pure network tariff.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to Verify Your 2027 Rate
The bill at the end of 2026 or early 2027 will bring the official rate update. However, you can anticipate this by reading the communication from your local distribution company. Every supplier must communicate the rates for the new year to the customer, clearly indicating: energy rate (in ct./kWh), network rate (in ct./kWh), metering rate (in CHF/year), fixed and variable supplements (winter reserve, levies, Swissgrid rates, etc.). If you receive the communication and the calculation is unclear to you, contact the customer service of the grid operator. Swiss regulations require full transparency in bills, and many operators also provide online calculators to estimate annual costs based on your consumption history.
ElCom has noted that improvements are needed in communications about tariff changes: often the justifications provided by operators are confusing and difficult to understand. If you notice this shortcoming, inform the operator of the need for clarification. The Federal Commission continues to monitor operators' compliance with communication and transparency requirements.
### Concrete Steps to Prepare for 2027
**1. Read the official communication.** The grid operator must communicate the new rates in writing at least one month before they take effect (January 2027). Keep this document for your tax and accounting records.
2. Compare with the previous year. Extract your November or December 2026 bill, note the current prices and compare them with the new ones. ElCom also publishes regional comparison data and data by consumption bracket.
3. Calculate your specific savings. If you consume 4,500 kWh annually (standard H4 profile), your savings will be close to 53 francs. If you consume less (e.g., 3,000 kWh) or more (e.g., 6,000 kWh), apply the simple calculation: 1.2 ct./kWh decrease × your annual kWh = savings in francs.
4. Check alternative supplier options. In Switzerland, the energy market has 'liberated' areas where you can choose your supplier. In Ticino, the market is liberalized for almost all household customers. If your current operator applies a rate significantly higher than the national or regional median, you can compare other offers and potentially switch operators.
### The Importance of Measurement Data Quality
ElCom emphasizes that the quality of measurement data is crucial not only for correctly billing consumption, but also to enable accurate forecasts of energy supply and demand at the national level and to avoid energy balancing costs. Incorrect data leads to system imbalances that then burden the rates of all consumers. If you notice anomalies in your bill (unexpectedly high consumption, double charges, inconsistently applied rates), report it immediately to the operator. Keep a copy of your complaint communication, and if the operator does not respond within the deadlines, you can escalate to the Federal Commission.
[Use our cost of living calculator](nav:cost-of-living) to assess the overall impact of the energy cost reduction on your Swiss household budget. Access updated national and regional data to understand how this reduction fits within the broader picture of your economic well-being and wealth management.
*Source: [admin.ch](https://www.admin.ch/it/newnsb/1miE201yRzoA)*

item.title: Swiss students read less: PISA 2025 results
item.description: PISA 2025: Swiss fifteen-year-olds excel in science, but reading and mathematics fall. 28.8% do not achieve minimum skills. The investigation reveals the crucial influence of social origin.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - PISA 2025: Switzerland declines in reading (-22 from 2015) and mathematics (-22) - Stable sciences and above OECD average: 501 points CH vs 482 OECD - Students with insufficient results growing: reading +8.8%, mathematics +7.4% - Social origin decisive: disadvantaged students report lower performance
## Key Facts - **What**: International PISA 2025 survey on school performance of fifteen-year-olds - When: Results released Tuesday from the University of Bern - Where: Switzerland, on behalf of the Confederation and Cantons - Who: University of Bern, conducted on federal and cantonal behalf - Reading: 470 points (vs 492 in 2015), OECD average 461 points - Mathematics: 499 points (vs 521 in 2015) - Sciences: 501 points (stable, vs 482 OECD) - Students with insufficient results in reading: 28.8% (vs 20% in 2015)
Performance in natural sciences remains stable and above the OECD average, but students with insufficient results are growing in mathematics as well. On Tuesday, the University of Bern released the results of the PISA 2025 survey on Swiss fifteen-year-olds: data that confirms the strength of the national school system in some areas, but highlights a concerning decline in reading and mathematics.
In natural sciences, young Swiss students achieved an average of 501 points, positioning themselves clearly above the OECD average of 482 points. This result confirms the stability of performance since 2015, when the score was already high. In the same period, the OECD average has declined steadily, widening the gap in Switzerland's favor.
### Reading and Mathematics in Decline
The picture changes significantly in reading and mathematics. In reading competence, the average value fell to 470 points from 2015, when it was 492 points. Despite the decline of 22 points, Switzerland is still above the OECD average of 461 points.
The negative trend repeats in mathematics: the score fell from 521 points in 2015 to 499 points in 2025. Here the loss of performance is even more marked: 22 points. However, Switzerland maintains a position of leadership at the international level in this area as well.
For model-based problem-solving, tested for the first time, Switzerland scored 520 points, a result above average. Moreover, in scientific-environmental competence, assessed for the first time in the survey, Switzerland achieved 495 points, always above the OECD average.
### The Paradox of Low-Performing Students
Although the international positioning remains strong, the growing number of students with insufficient results is emerging. In reading, the share of young people who did not reach minimum competencies rose from 20% in 2015 to 28.8% in 2025: an increase of 8.8 percentage points in a decade. This phenomenon has significant implications for [salaries](nav:calculator) and future economic prospects, given that lower skills correlate with lower incomes.
In mathematics, the trend is similar: the percentage of students with below-minimum performance has grown from 15.8% in 2015 to 23.2% in 2025, an increase of 7.4 percentage points. In natural sciences, instead, the share of young people with low performance remained stable at around 21%. This data reveals a polarization of the Swiss school system: while the best students maintain high levels of performance, a growing share of their peers falls behind in fundamental competencies. When compared to reference countries that are particularly relevant to Swiss educational policy, Switzerland consistently performs well. In natural sciences, only Estonia and Canada achieve better results in some sub-sectors. In mathematics, Switzerland stands out: only Estonia achieves even higher performance.
In reading, Estonia and Canada are ahead of Switzerland, while Finland and Italy reach a comparable level. This means that Switzerland, despite the decline, remains competitive with countries that historically excel in education. In model-based problem-solving, Switzerland is surpassed within the reference group only by Estonia, while Canada is statistically at the same level. Overall, Switzerland ranks among the top 20 countries out of 91 participants.
### The Influence of Social Background
A central finding of the study is the major influence that social background still exerts on academic success. Students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds achieved significantly worse results on average compared to their peers from privileged backgrounds.
This gap between privileged and disadvantaged young people peaked in 2022 but returned to 2015 levels in 2025. However, this apparent stabilization masks a worrying dynamic: the improvement does not reflect actual support for disadvantaged youth, but rather a decline in performance even among privileged students. In other words, the system has declined overall, rather than lifting the most vulnerable.
### Stability in Sciences, Decline in Reading and Mathematics
Stability in natural sciences contrasts sharply with declines in reading and mathematics. This suggests that the Swiss education system maintains strength in scientific fields, perhaps thanks to established curricula and methodologies, but has struggled in recent years to support basic linguistic and quantitative competencies.
The decline in reading is particularly significant given the central role of reading ability for success in all other disciplines. A student who cannot read fluently and with comprehension will face difficulties in mathematics, sciences, and humanities as well.
The increase in students with insufficient results implies a future challenge for Switzerland's [labor market](nav:jobs). Young people who today do not achieve minimum competencies risk encountering difficulties in finding qualified employment or progressing in the vocational training system.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). The PISA 2025 data represent a snapshot of school performance at national and international levels. For Swiss parents, the message is twofold: on one hand, the school system maintains global competitiveness; on the other, the growing number of struggling students suggests that not all young people receive the support necessary to achieve basic competencies.
If your son or daughter struggles with reading or mathematics, it is not an anomaly, but rather part of a national trend. This means that resources for school support (tutoring, remedial programs, differentiated pathways) should be a priority in the Cantons. Swiss schools, while remaining competitive internationally, need targeted interventions to reverse the trend.
### What Policy Makers Can Do
From the Confederation to the Cantons, these data represent a concrete call to action. Switzerland remains excellent in science and mathematics at the international level, but the downward trend in both areas requires attention. Policy makers will need to assess whether curricula are still suited to contemporary needs in reading and mathematics, whether teachers have updated methodologies, how to reduce the impact of social origin on performance, and what the plan is to reverse the negative trend by the next PISA cycle.
Switzerland is still among the 20 most performing countries of the 91 participants in the PISA 2025 survey. Maintaining this position requires strategic interventions and constant monitoring of the national educational trajectory.
### Concrete Next Steps
If you are parents, monitor your child's progress in reading and mathematics; do not hesitate to contact the school if you notice difficulties; ask for information about support programs available in your Canton.
To better understand the implications on [cost of living and quality of life in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), we invite you to consult the available resources. Furthermore, if you are interested in Swiss salaries and economic prospects, you can access our tools for a more complete view of the national landscape. The PISA 2025 data remind us that education remains one of the fundamental pillars of Swiss economic and social well-being.

item.title: BLS cuts 40 seats, closes centres and reduces services
item.description: BLS announces 40 job cuts, closure of 5 travel centres and reduced services. Target savings: CHF 5 million in the two-year period 2027-2028.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - BLS cuts 40 FTE positions in response to pressure on public transport costs - 5 travel centers close in the Canton of Bern, limited hours at 2 other counters - External train cleaning changes from every 14 days to once a month - On-board inspections reduced from 2028, target savings: 5 million CHF in 2027-2028 biennium
## Key Facts - **What**: Reduction of 40 jobs, closure of 5 travel centers, reduction of services - When: Implementation in the 2027-2028 biennium (inspections from 2028) - Where: Canton of Bern (Seftigen, Hasle-Rüegsau, Ins, Münsingen, Zollikofen; limitations at Spiez and Interlaken West) - Who: BLS (Bernese railway company) - Amount: Approximately 5 million CHF in projected savings - Lines affected: Bern-Langnau-Lucerne, Spiez-Zweisimmen
The railway company BLS announced today a reorganization plan that will significantly reduce staffing and services. The decision responds to growing economic pressure in the Swiss public transport sector, with pressure exerted by cantons and the Confederation on railway operators. This complex economic context forces railway operators to make difficult choices that directly impact the quality of employment and services.
The plan provides for the cut of approximately 40 full-time positions and the closure of five travel centers, all located in the Canton of Bern: Seftigen, Hasle-Rüegsau, Ins, Münsingen, and Zollikofen. Furthermore, opening hours of other counters at Spiez and Interlaken West will be limited, further reducing the availability of physical ticketing services for passengers. This strategy favors digital channels and automated machines, a choice that reflects modern trends but also impacts accessibility for those who prefer or need human interaction.
### Measures for reduction of services
The limitations will not stop at travel centers. BLS has planned a reduction in on-board inspections on the Bern-Langnau-Lucerne and Spiez-Zweisimmen lines starting from 2028. In parallel, external train cleaning will also undergo significant cuts: the frequency will change from every 14 days to once a month, a reduction that will have visible effects on regular fleet maintenance. This change in cleaning frequency could influence the perception of service quality among regular passengers.
With the implementation of these measures in the 2027-2028 biennium, BLS estimates savings of approximately 5 million francs. The company has clearly indicated that the cause is economic pressure in public transport, a sector where financial maneuverability has tightened in recent years. The unions immediately reacted negatively to the announcement. The Union of Transport Personnel (SEV) and the Transfair union both raised criticisms, considering that staff is the subject that pays the highest price for the reorganization. BLS's decision is not isolated within the Swiss context. Public transport faces structural economic challenges: management, maintenance, personnel, and energy costs continue to grow, while public funding from cantons and the Confederation remains under pressure. This financial squeeze creates a dynamic where railway operators must find internal efficiencies.
The Transport Personnel Union (SEV) described the situation by stating that 'cost pressure exerted by cantons and the Confederation is now having its first and drastic consequences'. This position reveals the crux of the problem: railway managers find themselves trapped between the need to maintain widespread public services and the reduction of public financial transfers. When these two factors clash, it is inevitable that something gives way.
### The position of unions and the impact on personnel
The Transfair union expanded the protest message, emphasizing that 'it is personnel who bear the costs of public sector cost-saving measures'. This statement embodies a recurrent trend in the debate on the sustainability of Swiss public transport: when external economic pressure is not accompanied by structural solutions, it is workers (and potentially passengers) who suffer the direct consequences.
The 40 positions cut by BLS do not represent a catastrophe in absolute terms for Swiss employment, but the signal is clear. The public transport sector, which has historically guaranteed job stability and professionalism, is going through a phase of stress that will lead to similar reorganizations at other operators. Union reactions signal a fundamental inconsistency: while public institutions reduce funding, they ask managers to maintain the quality of services, an expectation that is increasingly difficult to meet without cutting jobs. The BLS situation is therefore emblematic of a broader problem that involves the entire Swiss public transport system, from large companies like SBB to regional and cantonal operators.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). BLS measures will come into force starting from the 2027-2028 biennium, with the reduction of on-board checks confirmed from 2028. This schedule allows frequent travelers to plan adjustments and verify developments on BLS official channels. The company has already indicated that closures and schedule limitations will affect the centers in Seftigen, Hasle-Rüegsau, Ins, Münsingen, Zollikofen and partially Spiez and Interlaken West.
### How to organize with the new services
For those who depend on BLS for daily or occasional travel, the very first action is to consult the official BLS website to verify the status of your reference centers and the updated hours of the remaining open counters. The company has developed over the years a multi-channel strategy that includes the mobile app, online booking, automatic ticket dispensers and, of course, the possibility of purchasing travel tickets directly on board from staff (where still present).
In detail, the transition plan involves: immediate verification of your reference travel center if it is among the 5 that will close, migration to digital channels (BLS app, online portal, automats), advance planning of tickets especially for trips on critical lines (Bern-Langnau-Lucerne, Spiez-Zweisimmen), adjustment to the new on-board check frequencies from 2028.
For sector workers, the situation is more complex. The 40 job cuts will mainly affect operational and administrative profiles. Anyone working at BLS should maintain contact with their union representative or their reference union (SEV, Transfair) to understand if their position is at risk and what protection tools (training, internal mobility, wage subsidy) are available.
### Deadlines and monitoring
The complete timeline of implementations has not been made public in detail, but the 2027-2028 biennium represents the period of maximum transition. We recommend monitoring: December 2026/January 2027 for possible official BLS communications on center closures, 2027-2028 for the gradual implementation of organizational cuts, 2028 for the start of on-board check reduction on specific lines.
For a complete view of the impact on your travels, discover how to [organize your trips with Swiss public transport](nav:transport). item.title: Energy bills down 4% in 2027
item.description: ElCom announces the third consecutive year of decline. The average household will save CHF 53 per year, paying CHF 1,194 for energy.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief
- Electricity prices fall by 4% in 2027: average bill drops to 1,194 CHF annually - Savings of 53 francs for an average family consuming 4,500 kWh - Third consecutive year of decline following sharp increases in 2022–2024
## Key Facts
- **What**: Electricity price decline in Switzerland for 2027 - When: 2027 (4% reduction compared to 2026) - Who: Federal Electricity Commission (ElCom) - Where: All of Switzerland (with variation between providers) - Savings amount: 53 CHF annually per average family - Average bill 2027: 1,194 CHF - Cause: Reduction in energy procurement costs - Trend: Third consecutive year of decline
The Federal Electricity Commission (ElCom) announced on Tuesday a new decline in electricity prices for 2027. Rates will fall by 4% compared to the current year, confirming a downward trend that has now been ongoing for three years.
An average Swiss family consuming 4,500 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per year will pay 53 francs less than in 2026. The annual bill will therefore be around 1,194 francs. The figure, officially released by ElCom, represents a relief after years of tariff pressure that affected household budgets between 2022 and 2024.
### What caused the decline
The decline is primarily attributable to the reduction in energy procurement costs. However, ElCom emphasizes a crucial point: these are median values. Prices, in fact, vary considerably from one provider to another due to significant differences in supply, the energy source used, and network distribution costs.
### The context of the energy crisis
Until 2024, Switzerland faced an unprecedented energy crisis. Electricity prices skyrocketed during 2022–2023, creating shockwaves in household budgets. Since 2025, the trend has reversed: each year shows a consistent decline. This 2027 continues in that direction.
It should be noted, however, that the wholesale energy market is currently experiencing strong increases. According to ElCom, this volatility has virtually no impact on purchases already structured for the 2027 tariff year, as Swiss providers purchase energy well in advance. The consequences of current tensions in the international market will only be visible in coming years.
[Analyze the cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to understand the impact of your energy bill on your overall budget. ## Energy and household budget: practical implications
The 4% decline is not an abstract figure. For an average Swiss family, 53 francs in annual savings represents approximately 4-5 francs per month on an already stabilized bill. In terms of purchasing power, it is sufficient to cover other recurring expenses in the household budget or to add to emergency funds.
This relief comes at just the right time. The energy crisis of 2022–2023 had produced a double negative effect: substantial price increases and, in parallel, a reduction in economic confidence among Swiss consumers, who in many cases had to redirect resources toward heating and electricity. Three years of consecutive decline (2025, 2026, 2027) signal a return to tariff stability after the peak of volatility.
### Geographic variability and local providers
However, ElCom's data conceals an underestimated complexity. Prices vary considerably at the local level. A family living in the canton of Valais, where hydroelectricity is abundant, will pay significantly less than one in the canton of Geneva. Even within the same canton, the difference between local providers can be considerable. The 4% decline is a Swiss average: some customers will receive larger reductions, others smaller ones.
ElCom itself admits that prices sometimes vary considerably from one provider to another due to large differences in supply. This means that the annual benefit could range between 30 and 70 francs, rather than the 53 average.
### Small and medium-sized enterprises and network costs
An often overlooked aspect concerns small businesses and medium-sized enterprises. While energy prices fall for them too, network costs (including metering costs) are slightly increasing. This means that SMEs experience a smaller benefit compared to households. Network operators continue to invest in infrastructure and maintenance, translating these investments into tariffs that do not always decline in parallel with energy prices.
### Wholesale market and future volatility
The current rise in prices on the global wholesale market — influenced by geopolitical tensions and global macroeconomic factors — will not have an impact in 2027. But what will happen in 2028 and beyond? ElCom does not provide specific forecasts, but the signal is clear: external volatility continues to represent a structural risk. The coming years could bring upside surprises if international tensions persist or intensify. For this reason, fixed-price contracts could be strategic to protect the household budget from future fluctuations.
[Use the budget calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate exactly your annual energy savings based on your personal consumption and your region.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How to Monitor and Leverage the Tariff Reduction
The 4% reduction is not automatic. It depends on your local energy provider and the type of contract you have signed. Here is the procedure to ensure that the benefit applies to your bill.
### Verify Your Rate with Your Provider
The first step is to contact your regional network operator — the one shown on your bill. Provide them with your customer number (found in the document) and ask these questions:
- Does the 4% reduction announced by ElCom apply to my contract starting in 2027? - When does it come into effect exactly (usually starting from January 1st, but implementation varies)? - Are you on a fixed-price or variable-price contract?
If you have a fixed-price contract, the reduction may not apply until the contract expires. If you are on a variable-rate plan, the update typically occurs automatically at the beginning of the calendar year.
### Compare Providers (where possible in Switzerland)
Not all cantons allow switching energy providers. However, in those that permit choice, the 4% reduction may vary considerably among alternative providers. Check if your region offers energy market liberalization:
- Check the website of the main provider in your area for information on switching possibilities - If choice is available, compare 2027 rates from at least two providers before deciding - Remember that switching has minimal administrative costs but requires a few days of processing
### Calculate Your Personalized Savings
The savings of 53 CHF is calculated on a standard consumption of 4,500 kWh. If you consume less (small apartment, no electric heating), savings will be proportionally lower. Example: 3,000 kWh = approximately 35 CHF in savings. If you consume more energy (electric heating, heat pump), savings will be higher. Example: 6,000 kWh = approximately 70 CHF annually.
Check your last three bills to calculate your average annual consumption, then apply the 4% reduction rate to estimate your personal benefit.
### Plan Your 2027 Budget
The 53 CHF annual reduction may seem modest, but it is part of a broader household budget. In the general context of the cost of living in Switzerland, every recurring saving counts. Consider reinvesting this margin in other priorities — rent, health insurance, emergency fund — or using it for other home investments (energy efficiency, insulation, heat pumps).
### Stay Updated on Rates
ElCom regularly publishes official announcements on electricity prices for the year. Check the ElCom website for official annual communications on national rates. Additionally, your local provider must inform customers at least 30 days before any significant rate changes.
[Use the budget calculator](nav:calculator) to track your annual energy costs and verify whether the 4% reduction is reflected in your monthly spending estimate.

item.description: In 2027 electricity rates fall by 4% according to Elcom. A typical household saves CHF 53 per year, but regional variations remain significant.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Rates down 4% in 2027, average CHF 53 annual savings per household - A household consuming 4,500 kWh will pay CHF 26.45/kWh in 2027 - Elcom announced the new rates on Tuesday; they vary between municipalities and network operators - Check online your network operator's rate by end of August
## Key facts - **What**: General decline in electricity rates in Switzerland - When: Starting January 1, 2027 - Where: Entire Switzerland (variations by canton and network operator) - Who: Elcom (Swiss Federal Electricity Commission) - Percentage: -4% national average - Annual savings: CHF 53 for a typical household - Reference consumption: 4,500 kWh/year - Average 2027 price: CHF 26.45/kWh
The Swiss Federal Electricity Commission (Elcom), Switzerland's regulatory authority, announced on Tuesday the electricity price verdict for 2027: an average 4 percent decrease compared to 2026. In concrete terms, a household consuming 4,500 kilowatt-hours per year will pay 26.45 cents per kilowatt-hour, which is 1.2 cents less than the current year, for an annual total of 1,194 francs. This decline translates to savings of approximately 53 francs on year-end electricity bills.
This decrease comes after a period of pronounced volatility. In 2026, compared to 2025, the rate had already fallen 4 percent. In 2025, the decline was even steeper, at 10 percent. These two years of reduction have partially offset the significant increases recorded in 2023 and 2024, when shocks in European energy markets had substantially raised electricity costs for Swiss consumers. Rates have now stabilized at an elevated level, but the trend is clearly downward.
### The composition of the decline and territorial variations
The decrease is primarily due to falling energy prices on international markets. According to Elcom, the actual energy tariff will decline, while network costs (infrastructure) and measurement fees will increase. For medium-sized businesses, the picture is similar.
Although the national average drops 4 percent, the overall figure masks significant variations between network operators and municipalities. The main reason lies in differences in the energy mix: some municipalities source power mainly from local hydroelectric plants (stable cost), while others depend on contracts in the European wholesale market (more exposed to volatility). Some operators adopt forward purchasing strategies, while others prefer greater flexibility in the spot market. These choices result in deviations of several cents per kilowatt-hour between regions, and even between adjacent municipalities.
Around 580 distribution network operators in Switzerland were required by end of August to communicate their 2027 rates to Elcom and customers. It is possible to check online the specific rates for your municipality on Elcom's official electricity prices website. This transparency makes it possible to verify whether your operator is in line with the national average or charges higher rates. ### What Changes in the Bill Structure
The electricity bill consists of three elements: the energy tariff (the price of gross kWh), network costs (transport and distribution), and the metering tariff (meter management). In 2027, the energy component will decrease thanks to more favorable prices on global markets, but network costs will continue to rise. This phenomenon is not accidental: network operators are investing in stabilization infrastructure (transition to distributed photovoltaic, storage, smart grid) and these costs are gradually passed on to customers.
For families and small businesses, the crucial point is that the net balance 2026→2027 is positive: they will pay less than before, even if the margins of decline are narrowing. Prospects for 2028 and beyond will depend on geopolitical developments and European energy prices.
### The Trend from 2023 to 2027
Historical analysis clearly shows the path of Swiss consumers in recent years. In 2023 and 2024, increases were significant due to the European energy crisis and market volatility. In 2025, the first major decline of 10 percent marked the beginning of stabilization. In 2026, the decline solidified at 4 percent, and the same will continue in 2027. Elcom emphasizes that tariffs have now stabilized at a high level compared to the pre-2022 period, which means that although consumers pay less this year, they remain in a more expensive range compared to the recent past.
For those who want to estimate their annual consumption and understand how spending varies with different usage habits, our [calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to enter the number of people in your household and main appliances to get a realistic estimate.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to check your provider's rates
If you live in Switzerland and want to know exactly what rate you'll pay in 2027, the process is simple and straightforward:
1. **Access the official website** — Visit the Elcom electricity price website (or the equivalent cantonal platform) 2. Enter your postal code and municipality — The system identifies the network operator responsible for your area 3. Select your provider — If multiple operators work in your municipality, choose the correct one from the menu 4. Check the 2027 rate — The price in cents per kWh will already be displayed (by end of August 2026) 5. Compare with the average — Compare your data with the 26.45 cents/kWh national average to understand if you're in a high-cost area
This verification is also useful for those living in cantons with partial market liberalization (Zurich, Basel, St. Gallen, Geneva, Thurgau). In some regions it's possible to change energy supplier while staying with the same network operator; in other cantons the network operator remains a monopoly.
### When the new rates come into effect
The 2027 rates come into effect on January 1, 2027. Operators will communicate the details in the end-of-2026 bill or early 2027, with comparison tables for 2026 vs 2027. If you notice an abnormal increase compared to the national average, verify if your operator works in a region with significantly higher network costs.
Because the latest Elcom data clearly shows that an average family will find relief in their 2027 bill. The discount is modest (53 francs per year) but concrete, and represents the second consecutive year of decline after the difficult increases of 2023-2024.
If you want to plan your energy budget and understand the impact of electricity costs on your overall income, use our [calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate consumption and expenses based on your family profile and usage habits.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/svizzera/economia/1948713/tariffe-elettricita-prezzi-franchi-elcom)*

item.title: Volkswagen cuts 50,000, AMAG reassures customers
item.description: Volkswagen cuts 50,000 seats. Amag reassures: no employment impact, stable prices and leadership in the electric car with Skoda.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Volkswagen announces the largest restructuring plan in its history with 50,000 new job cuts - Amag reassures Swiss customers: no impact on employment and leadership in the electric segment - Skoda is the leading brand for electric vehicle sales in Switzerland, VW absolute leader with share >31%
## Key Facts - **Who**: Helmut Ruhl, CEO Amag (Swiss importer of Volkswagen) - What: Volkswagen announces restructuring (50,000 cuts + 100,000 total), halving of models, possible plant closures - When: Announcement last Friday - Where: Zurich (Amag), Swiss car market - Market share: Amag holds >31% of the Swiss market; Volkswagen 28th most purchased brand - E-car: Skoda first for electric vehicle sales in Switzerland
Volkswagen announced last Friday the largest restructuring plan in its history, with approximately 50,000 new job cuts (for a total of around 100,000), the halving of models and the possible closure of several plants. An announcement that could have thrown Swiss customers into uncertainty, but which the local importer Amag immediately countered with a statement of absolute reassurance.
CEO Helmut Ruhl emphasized in an interview published by 20 Minuten that Volkswagen products and services are 'future-proof'. The reduction of personnel at the German giant, Ruhl assured, will have no impact on Amag's employment situation. Indeed: the company reiterated that it is an independent Swiss family business and highlighted how Volkswagen's measures will, in the long term, help safeguard jobs in the Swiss supplier industry, traditionally closely linked to the German and European automotive sector.
### Volkswagen's Plan and Strategic Implications
Ruhl positively assessed the German group's austerity package, particularly the choice to halve the model range and the focus on differentiation through software rather than hardware. According to the manager, these steps represent a 'necessary adjustment of capacities to the new market conditions'.
On the front of electric mobility, Amag's number one categorically rejected the accusation that Volkswagen has lost ground compared to Chinese competition, particularly compared to players like BYD. 'Absolutely not', Ruhl said. 'The situation in Switzerland is not comparable to that of the Chinese car market.' He emphasized that Volkswagen electric cars charge faster and have greater range. Amag claims leadership in the segment of purely electric vehicles, with Skoda as the leading brand for e-car sales in the Confederation. According to the importer, demand for new models remains very strong. ### Volkswagen's Dominance in the Swiss Market
Despite the global turbulence surrounding Volkswagen, the group maintains a position of absolute dominance in the Swiss automotive market. Last year, Volkswagen was for the 28th time the most purchased brand in the Confederation, while Skoda ranks in second place. As of this year, Skoda has established itself as the manufacturer that sells the most electric cars in Switzerland, a primacy that shows how the VW group, despite global difficulties, knows how to interpret the preferences of the local market.
Amag, the importer, claims a market share of over 31%, a position of strength that allows it to speak with credible voice to over 2 million Swiss residents. Chinese competition, with brands like BYD in strong growth in Europe, is monitored with attention, but Amag is convinced of remaining firmly in command. As Ruhl clarified, the Volkswagen brand is now synonymous with German quality and reliability: according to a study conducted by the Sotomo research institute in July, Germany is the preferred country of origin for purchasing a vehicle, with 84% preference among Swiss people.
### Reassurances on Prices and Deliveries
A natural concern among consumers is whether VW's downsizing plan will lead to price increases or delays in deliveries. On both fronts, Ruhl offered explicit guarantees. The prices charged in Switzerland, he clarified, derive from the competitive situation in the local market and are independent of Volkswagen's internal decisions. On this point, it remains relevant to understand the dynamics of costs in the Swiss market to understand how automotive transactions fit into the general economy.
As for delivery times, Amag reassured that there will be no negative consequences. The operator will continue to offer the usual complete service, including the fastest possible delivery of ordered vehicles. Regarding the reduction of the model range, Ruhl argued that a simplification of the offer brings advantages to customers, such as greater clarity, availability and efficiency in services.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What does it mean for Swiss customers and consumers
Amag's reassurance directly addresses the doubts of those considering buying a Volkswagen car. The CEO directly addressed the legitimate question: 'Does it still make sense to buy a Volkswagen automobile?' The answer was categorical and articulated. Ruhl emphasized that many new automotive brands still need to establish themselves in the tough competition of the Swiss market, and that some will not succeed. Mid-year, he recalled, Volkswagen remains the world's largest automotive group in terms of revenue, second in sales and third in economic profit.
For customers, what truly matters are concrete elements: attractive products, consistent quality, reliable after-sales service, parts availability, and value retention over time. On all these fronts, according to Ruhl, Volkswagen and the group as a whole remain undisputed leaders in the Swiss market.
### What to do now
If you own a Volkswagen or Skoda car in Switzerland, or are considering buying one, Amag's statements offer solidity and predictability. The message is clear: Volkswagen's downsizing plan is an internal measure by the German group, necessary to adapt to global market conditions, but does not affect the continuity of service, quality, and car availability in the Swiss market.
The practical implications for those living or working in Switzerland are minimal in terms of immediate constraints. There are no deadlines to meet, no particular procedures to follow, nor new federal or cantonal regulations to comply with. What remains is the freedom to choose among Volkswagen, Skoda, and Audi brands present in Switzerland, with the assurance that the local importer Amag will continue to provide the service and support that consumers are accustomed to.
For those interested in understanding how car purchase fits into the overall [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), a useful resource remains the comparative evaluation of total cost of ownership. Similarly, for those considering a job or sector change within the automotive industry and suppliers, the [Swiss job market](nav:jobs) continues to offer opportunities despite global uncertainties.
For a precise net salary calculation, use our [tax comparator](nav:calculator): compare take-home pay between G and B permits with all 2026 deductions.

item.title: Petrol and diesel shortage: compulsory stocks taken
item.description: Cressier refinery stopped due to failure, limited Rhine transport. Authorized withdrawals of 30,000 m³ of gasoline and diesel between 8-20 September from mandatory stocks.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - Cressier refinery shut down due to technical fault, supply under pressure - Authorization to withdraw 30,000 m³ of petrol and 30,000 m³ of diesel from September 8 to 20 - Quantities represent less than 3% of total mandatory reserves
## Key facts - **What**: Withdrawal from mandatory reserves of petrol and diesel on federal authorization - When: September 8–20, 2026 - Where: Switzerland, Cressier refinery (Canton Neuchâtel) - Who: Roland Pfister, delegate for Economic Supply - Amount: 30,000 m³ petrol + 30,000 m³ diesel - Percentage: Less than 3% for each product - Coverage: Mandatory reserves cover approximately 4.5 months of average demand - Replenishment: Within 6 months of the measure's revocation
The fuel supply situation in Switzerland has deteriorated in recent days. Roland Pfister, the Country's delegate for Economic Supply, has authorized the use of mandatory reserves of petrol and diesel from September 8 to 20 to ensure the continuity of supplies across the national territory. The withdrawal amounts to 30,000 cubic meters of petrol and 30,000 cubic meters of diesel. Although it may seem like a considerable figure, it represents less than 3% of the respective mandatory reserves for each of the two products.
### What caused the crisis
The Cressier refinery, in Canton Neuchâtel, is the only active refinery in Switzerland. Last week, it temporarily halted production due to a technical fault. It normally covers just over 30% of Switzerland's demand for petroleum products. The facility is expected to return to operations around mid-September, but in the meantime the market is under extraordinary pressure. The situation has been further complicated by water scarcity in the Rhine. Low water levels have drastically reduced river transport capacity, an essential method for fuel supply to Switzerland. Rail transport is already heavily strained, and the pipeline connecting France to Geneva cannot compensate for either the quantity or the timing of the deficit caused by the refinery's shutdown.
### Details of the measure
The stated objective of the measure is to support the market during the period of difficulty and ensure the continuity of the Country's supply. Monitoring the impact on your economic situation during this phase is important, as any price variations could be reflected in your personal and business budget. The quantities withdrawn from reserves must be replenished within six months of the measure's revocation. Should the situation extend beyond expectations, further withdrawals may be authorized. The refinery shutdown mainly affects petrol and diesel. For the moment, no difficulties are reported in the supply of heating oil and kerosene, which maintain a more stable situation compared to transport fuels. ### How mandatory stockpiles work
Mandatory stockpiles represent a strategic buffer to ensure the security of national supply. In the case of petrol and diesel, they belong to companies and generally allow to cover approximately four and a half months of average demand for each product. This is a collective resource managed through a federal authorization system. Recourse to reserves is not new: when a temporary supply shortage occurs, the country's delegate for economic supply has the power to authorize the release of up to 20% of the mandatory stockpiles of a given product.
### Role of the Confederation and competencies
This is an exclusive competency of the federal delegate for amounts up to 20%. If withdrawals exceeded this threshold, competency would pass to the Federal Department of Economy, Education and Research (SERI), which must authorize recourse through a federal ordinance. In the case of the current crisis, the authorized amounts (30,000 m³ per product) remain below the 20% threshold of total stockpiles, thus allowing delegate Pfister to decide independently without needing to involve SERI through a formal ordinance. This mechanism allows for a rapid response to emergencies without procedural delays.
### Duration and replenishment
The measure was conceived as circumscribed in time and temporary. The authorization period is set until September 20, with the hope that production at the Cressier refinery can resume as planned. However, the regulatory framework provides that if the situation were to persist beyond what was initially estimated, further withdrawals could be authorized through new ordinances. The quantities used must be replenished within six months from the revocation of the measure. This means that the companies owning the stockpiles will have a reasonable period to replenish strategic reserves, presumably through imports or resumption of domestic production. Fluctuations in fuel availability and prices can significantly impact your personal and business economic situation. [Use the cost of living calculator](nav:cost-of-living) to monitor how these fluctuations affect your budget.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What does it mean concretely for citizens and businesses
Mandatory fuel reserves are designed to prevent tangible fuel shortages in the coming days. Although the measure does not guarantee an immediate return to normal prices, it should prevent situations where petrol and diesel are unavailable at gas stations in Switzerland. For transport and distribution companies, the measure provides relief during the refinery shutdown. However, it is possible that during the shortage period (until 20 September) retail price variations may be observed due to reduced availability and increased concentrated demand.
### When and where to get information
Official communications on the supply status are published by federal institutional channels, particularly by the delegate for Economic Supply and the Federal Department of Economics, Education and Research. National media disseminate regular updates on refinery recovery and the overall situation. If the refinery does not return to operation by mid-September as planned, it is likely that the Swiss government will communicate new emergency measures, possibly resorting to further withdrawals from reserves. In that case, federal ordinances will communicate any changes promptly.
### Next steps and practical strategies
In the meantime, for those who regularly use petrol or diesel, it is advisable to monitor official communications and refuel when availability levels permit, avoiding letting tanks drop too low. For companies, directly consulting their usual suppliers about possible delivery limitations or price variations remains the most prudent strategy. The situation should normalize once the refinery has completed the repair of the technical fault, probably by mid-September according to current forecasts. However, even once restarted, internal production will need to compensate for the deficit accumulated during the shutdown and transport difficulties on the Rhine will continue to affect supply times until water levels return to normal.
In the medium term, river transport difficulties remain a critical factor. The low Rhine limits the inherent capacity for fuel movement, a bottleneck that cannot be quickly resolved. For this reason, supply monitoring will remain a priority even after production restoration at Cressier. If you wish to follow the impact of these federal decisions on your personal or business economic situation, [use our cost of living calculator](nav:cost-of-living) to estimate the impact of any price variations on your consumption and family budget.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/svizzera/economia/1948704/carenza-di-benzina-e-gasolio-si-attinge-alle-scorte-obbligatorie)*

item.title: Ticino School: PISA 2025 results down
item.description: In 2025 Ticino remained in the top 10 OECD in mathematics but lost points. 27.2% of fifteen-year-olds do not reach the minimum reading level.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - PISA 2025: Ticino among the top 10 OECD countries in mathematics (492 points vs 463) - All disciplines declining since 2022: reading -24.1 points - 27.2% of fifteen-year-olds below the minimum level in reading - Sample composition changed: +4.5% students still in lower secondary
## Key facts - **What**: PISA 2025 survey on mathematics, reading and science competences - When: 2025 (comparison with 2022 and historical data since 2015) - Where: Ticino, on a sample of 91 participating countries - Who: CIRSE of SUPSI on behalf of DECS - Scores: Mathematics 492 (OECD 463), reading 470 (OECD 461), science 492 (OECD 482)
Ticino maintains top positions in the PISA 2025 international ranking, placing itself among the top ten in mathematics and among the top twenty in science and reading. However, the results show a clear decline compared to 2022: mathematics loses 22.9 points, reading 24.1 and science 16.5. The survey, conducted every three years on girls and boys around 15 years old, was carried out by the Centre for Competence, Innovation and Research on Educational Systems (CIRSE) of SUPSI on behalf of the Department of Education, Culture and Sport (DECS). In 2025, a module dedicated to learning in the digital world was added.
In absolute terms, Ticino records 492 points in mathematics against 463 of the OECD average—a statistically significant difference. In reading, the Ticino result is 470 points, in line with the OECD average of 461 and with the Swiss one, also at 470. In science, the main focus of the 2025 edition, the Ticino score is 492 points, higher than 482 of the OECD average. Compared to Switzerland (501 points), Ticino falls by nine points, but the difference is not statistically significant.
### The concerning data: reading
The most critical aspect concerns the level of reading competence. As many as 27.2% of Ticino fifteen-year-olds do not reach level 2, considered by the OECD as the minimum threshold necessary to cope with everyday situations. In science and mathematics, the proportions are lower: 20.3% and 24.4% respectively. The data on reading is alarming when observed historically: in 2015 the percentage of young Ticino residents below level 2 in reading was 16.4%, which means an increase of almost 11 percentage points in a decade.
Reading is not an isolated competence: it is transversal to all other disciplines. Understanding the language of a mathematics question, identifying relevant information or formulating complex reasoning depend on language mastery. A deficit here compromises learning in every subject. Among the 91 countries participating in the survey, Ticino nonetheless maintains a prominent position. In mathematics it ranks among the top ten; in science and reading among the top twenty. ### Sample composition: a decisive factor
Before interpreting the decline as a simple erosion of skills, one crucial element must be considered: the composition of the sample changed significantly between the two surveys. Between 2022 and 2025, the share of fifteen-year-olds attending secondary II fell from 81.4% to 76.9%. At the same time, the proportion of pupils still in secondary school increased from 18.6% to 23.1%. This means that, in 2025, a greater portion of fifteen-year-olds from Ticino took the test while still in secondary I, with an overall shorter school course than their peers already in secondary II.
The DECs considers it necessary to deepen this element, as it could have had a significant impact on the overall scores. A student who is still in middle school will presumably have accumulated fewer teaching hours in disciplines such as math and science than one already in high school II. This variable may explain some, if not all, of the observed contraction.
The downward trend is not exclusive to Ticino. The same contraction is observed at the Swiss level and in the OECD average, suggesting a broader structural phenomenon. However, for Ticino, it remains a priority to understand whether the decline is due to demographic changes in the sample or to a real decrease in pedagogical skills.
### Positives: Equity and Excellence
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Perspectives and Implications for the Education System
PISA 2025 results raise relevant questions for educational policies at the cantonal level. The contraction of scores, particularly in reading, suggests the need for targeted interventions in text comprehension. This is not just an isolated school problem. Reading is a key competency also in the Swiss labor market, where professions increasingly require the ability to process complex information, technical documentation, and written communication.
The DECS will need to assess whether the causes lie in demographic changes in the sample (larger share of lower secondary students) or in actual pedagogical factors. Once these aspects are clarified, specific interventions can be designed: strengthening reading instruction in middle schools, curriculum review, teacher training, or innovative use of digital tools. The module added in 2025 dedicated to learning in the digital world already represents a step in this direction.
The generalized decline—also at Swiss and OECD level—suggests that Ticino is not isolated in this challenge. It is possible that global factors (residual effects of the pandemic, changes in learning environments, more intensive use of devices) have played a role. The internal DECS task force will therefore need to analyze both national and international data as well as data specific to Ticino to design a balanced strategy.
### Monitoring and Available Tools

item.title: Swiss economy Q2 2026: +5.3% turnover, +2% employment
item.description: In Q2 2026, Swiss market branches grow: turnover +5.3%, employment +2.0%. Tertiary driving with +8.5%, trade +12.2%.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - In Q2 2026, turnover +5.3%, employment +2.0% in Swiss sectors - Tertiary (services) leads with +8.5% revenue; trade +12.2% - Energy sector expands employment (+2.4%) but production declines (-2.0%)
## Key Facts - **What**: Economic and employment growth in Swiss market sectors - When: Second quarter 2026 (press release September 8, 2026) - Where: Swiss market sectors at national level - Who: FSO (Federal Statistical Office), FEO (Energy) - Amount: +5.3% turnover, +2.0% overall employment
### Broad-based Growth in Q2 2026
In the second quarter of 2026, Switzerland's market-oriented economic sectors showed broad-based expansion. According to FSO data, turnover increased by 5.3% compared to the same quarter in 2025, while employment grew by 2.0% — in line with the increase in total national employment.
The secondary sector (industry and construction) recorded more modest growth: turnover advanced by 0.4% and employment by 1.2%. Within it, industry experienced a slight contraction in turnover (-0.3%), while employment in this sector grew by 0.9%. Construction, by contrast, showed dynamism: turnover increased by 3.1% and employment by 1.7%.
The tertiary sector (services) led overall growth, with turnover up 8.5% and employment up 2.4% compared to Q2 2025.
### Trade Dominance, Employment Caution
Among tertiary sectors, trade posted the best performance: turnover +12.2%, the highest among all economic sectors. However, employment in trade fell by 0.2%. In retail specifically, turnover grew by 1.1% and employment by 0.3%.
Similarly, 'Information and communication' saw employment contract by -3.1%. The 'Administrative activities and support services' section recorded the strongest employment growth in the tertiary sector: +10.5%, reflecting strong demand for support services to Swiss businesses.
These data suggest that economic growth is accompanied by a reconfiguration of employment: some sectors grow in revenue but not in jobs, while others significantly expand their workforce. ### The employment boom in the energy sector
The energy supply sector (supply of electricity, gas and steam via network — NOGA 35), while being part of the secondary sector, has followed a very different path from that of industry over the past ten years. Between Q2 2016 and Q2 2026, employment in full-time equivalents increased by 27.1%, a growth significantly higher than the secondary sector overall (+6.0%). From 2021 onwards, employment growth has been even more dramatic: +20.8% in the energy sector compared to +5.4% in the secondary sector.
However, this employment boom is not accompanied by production growth. Over the decade 2016-2026, real production in the energy sector declined by 10.2%, while the secondary sector recorded an increase of 35.4%. Nominal revenue figures tell a different story: they increased by 35.5% in the energy sector (in line with the +35.3% in the secondary sector) and from 2021 as much as 41.6%, compared to +19.0% in the secondary sector.
This divergence clarifies the driver of economic growth in the energy sector: it is energy prices, not the volumes produced or sold, that drive the increase in revenue figures. The Federal Office of Energy (UFE) provides the production and consumption data that underlie this phenomenon.
### Year-on-year contraction, quarterly recovery
Looking at the most recent period (Q2 2026 vs Q2 2025), the energy sector presents a less rosy picture. Employment continued to grow by 2.4% (in line with the +1.2% in the secondary sector), but production fell by -2.0% and revenue by -8.7% — in contrast with the secondary sector, which recorded production growth of 5.1% and stable revenue (+0.4%).
However, moving from Q1 to Q2 2026, net of seasonal variations, the energy sector shows signs of recovery. Production rose by 4.5% and revenue by 1.9%, though still below the results of the secondary sector (+7.7% production, +4.1% revenue). Employment recorded a slight quarterly decline (-0.3%), while in the secondary sector it marked a slight increase (+0.3%).
These fluctuations suggest that the energy sector remains sensitive to price and demand fluctuations, with an increasingly robust employment structure despite the volatility of volumes.

For those working in Switzerland or managing a company, understanding these sectoral trends helps assess the strength of one's sector and employment prospects.
The aggregate figure — +5.3% turnover and +2.0% employment — suggests an expanding economy, but variability by sector is marked. Those operating in retail witness modest growth (+1.1% revenue, +0.3% jobs), while the administrative and support sector sees strong employment expansion (+10.5%). UST provides detailed data on its official website, enabling in-depth analysis by canton, economic sector, and qualification. Job seekers, those changing sectors, or evaluating new positions should consult employment data for their industry: a 10.5% increase (as in administrative services) indicates growing demand, while a decline (-3.1% in Information and Communication) suggests greater selectivity in hiring processes.

item.title: Serious injuries: almost 90% return to work
item.description: Suva: After serious accidents, 90% of policyholders return to work. 78% return within 3 months thanks to medical care and personalised case management.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Suva recognized almost 480,000 workplace accidents in the past year - 90% of insured persons return to work after serious accidents - 78% return within three months; 6% face longer absences
## Key Facts - **Who**: Suva (Swiss Federal Accident Insurance) - What: Professional reintegration rates following serious workplace accidents - When: Past year; 2,400 people in case management in 2025 - Where: Switzerland; specialized clinics in Bellikon and Sion - Reintegration rate: 88%, stable year-on-year - Serious accidents: 29,000 out of 480,000 (disability >3 months) - Average return: 44 days; 78% within 3 months
Suva recognized almost 480,000 workplace accidents over the past year. Of these, approximately 29,000 were so serious that they caused work incapacity lasting more than three months. Despite the severity of many cases, nearly 90% of insured persons involved in serious accidents managed to return to work, thanks to effective medical care, professional support, and the backing of those close to them.
### The recovery path is long, but timeliness is crucial
A workplace accident can happen in an instant: a moment of distraction, a fall, or an unforeseen event can change one's daily life. However, the recovery and reintegration path into professional life is often long and demanding. Studies show that after six months of absence from work, the chances of returning are cut in half, making timely intervention by Suva and all the figures involved in the process essential.
Suva is committed from the outset to promoting a return to normalcy. Nearly half of recognized accidents resulted in work absence lasting more than three days, with an overall average of 44 days of work incapacity. 78% of injured workers returned within three months, a figure that highlights the effectiveness of timely interventions. 6% instead faced longer periods of absence, often due to injuries from falls affecting knees, shoulders, ankles, or the back — areas that require longer rehabilitation times and specific rehabilitation interventions. ### The fundamental role of Suva case management
For the most complex cases, Suva activates its own case management: case managers coordinate care, rehabilitation and return to work, collaborating with doctors, employers and other social insurances. In 2025, 2,400 people were followed through this service, a significant number of professionals who benefit from a structured and personalized accompaniment during the healing and reintegration process.
A key role is played by the clinics of Bellikon and Sion, which specialise in post-traumatic rehabilitation and professional reintegration. These facilities bring together medical, rehabilitation and professional skills to address the most complex cases, offering integrated programs that go beyond simple medical care and involve both physical healing and preparation for return to work.
### What is meant by successful reinstatement
The rate of professional reintegration of Suva policyholders after a serious accident stands at 88%, a figure that has remained stable over the years, confirming the effectiveness of the integrated approach. Reintegration is considered successful when the person returns to their job or finds a new one without the need for a disability pension, or with a pension of less than 20%. This 20% threshold represents the boundary between a functional return and a situation that still requires social security support.
Barbara
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Personal network support is as important as medical care
Fundamental to the recovery process, alongside care and professional support from Suva, is the support of one's personal network: family, friends, colleagues, and employers play a crucial role in the healing process, offering strength and confidence during difficult times. Many injured individuals report that the emotional and practical support from those around them was decisive in overcoming the most critical phases of rehabilitation and return to work.
Sandro Michel, former professional athlete and bobsledder, suffered a serious accident in 2024 and was able to count on the support of his personal network and Suva, demonstrating how the combination of institutional and personal resources can produce concrete results. "I am incredibly grateful for the support I received. Without all these people, I wouldn't be where I am today," Michel explains, illustrating how reintegration is not purely a technical process, but also an emotional and relational one.
### Concrete procedure after a serious accident
When a serious accident occurs with prolonged work incapacity, the procedure to follow is as follows: Suva automatically opens the injured person's file and organizes initial medical care; within the first few months, if a complex situation emerges, a dedicated case manager is activated; the case manager coordinates with the treating physician, the employer, and the injured person a personalized rehabilitation plan; if necessary, the case can be referred to specialized clinics in Bellikon or Sion; during recovery, work capacity is periodically evaluated and reintegration programs are adjusted; the goal is to return to the original job, and if that's not possible, alternatives consistent with remaining capacity are sought.
The promptness of intervention is crucial: the faster the reintegration plan is initiated, the greater the chances of success, as demonstrated by data showing that 78% return within three months. For those in this situation, it is essential to maintain constant communication with Suva, doctors, and the employer, without giving up at the first obstacle.
