item.title: CHFD digital franc: tests with 9 companies are underway
item.description: The CHFD digital franc is undergoing practical testing with 9 companies until the end of 2026. The applications examined range from automatic payments to managing digital assets on blockchain.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - CHFD is a stablecoin worth exactly 1 Swiss franc (CHF) - Practical test with 9 companies through end of 2026 in a protected environment - Blockchain transactions; payments and digital assets under examination
## Key Facts - **What**: Digital franc CHFD (stablecoin pegged to CHF) - When: Operational since end of June 2026, testing through end of 2026 - Where: Project coordinated at Swiss national level - Who: 9 companies including UBS, PostFinance, SIX, Twint, Sygnum, Raiffeisen, ZKB, BCV, Swiss Stablecoin AG - Ratio: 1 CHFD = 1 CHF - Technology: Blockchain for verified transactions
Nine Swiss companies have launched practical tests of the digital franc (CHFD) as a stablecoin, an innovative tool announced last April. The project involves major banks such as UBS and PostFinance, regional institutions (Sygnum, Raiffeisen, Zürcher Kantonalbank, BCV), the Swiss Stablecoin AG platform, stock exchange operator SIX, and payment app Twint. This representative cross-section of the Swiss financial system is working in parallel to define concrete applications for a national digital currency.
CHFD is technically operational since the end of June and is pegged to the Swiss franc at a one-to-one ratio: one CHFD corresponds to one Swiss franc (CHF). Transactions occur via blockchain, a digital ledger in which operations are recorded and jointly verified by multiple computers, ensuring transparency and security. The pilot program will continue until the end of 2026 in a protected digital environment — no citizens or companies outside the nine participants can access or directly test it at this stage.
### Which applications are being examined?
The tests focus on concrete areas of the Swiss financial system and payments. Among the applications being examined are automated payments between financial institutions (fundamental for the efficiency of bank settlement) and the management of digital assets (securities, contracts, digital goods). Participants also intend to verify whether programmable payments — transactions that execute automatically when certain conditions are met — can prevent fraud in online markets, enable fairer ticket sales for events, or be used for public authority payments (for example, tax payments, municipal fees). Learn how to best manage your [tax return](nav:tax-return) in Switzerland.
This pragmatic approach reflects Swiss interest in testing digital currency in real-world scenarios of the financial system before any decision on a general public launch. ### How Does CHFD Work and Why Is Switzerland Experimenting With It?
Digital franc represents a technological evolution of Swiss currency. Unlike volatile cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin, Ethereum), a stablecoin is anchored to a fixed value — in this case the CHF franc. This ensures stability and allows it to be used in contexts where volatility would be a problem: recurring payments between companies, recurring commercial transactions, payments to public entities, settlement of commercial contracts.
Switzerland has chosen to experiment with CHFD with nine financial and technological players — a representative sample of the national financial system from major banks to innovative payment services. Blockchain enables verified, transparent transactions that are potentially faster than traditional centralized settlement systems used today (such as SIC or Swiss Interbank Clearing). Every operation remains recorded and verifiable, reducing fraud risks and increasing efficiency.
### What Concrete Advantages for the Swiss Financial System?
For [Swiss banks](nav:banks) and payment services, CHFD opens concrete scenarios. Automated payments between financial institutions could significantly reduce current settlement times, accelerating cash flows for companies. The management of digital assets could facilitate the trading of securities, bonds, and smart contracts in a faster and more transparent way, without paper intermediaries.
Programmable payments deserve particular attention. A programmable transaction would allow: automatic execution when a condition is verified (for example: 'pay CHF 50 when you receive delivery confirmation') — reducing fraud risk in online sales; fairer access to limited resources, with concert or event tickets sold fairly through transparent algorithms rather than through manual 'click race', guaranteeing equal opportunities for all; automation of public payments with payments of municipal taxes, concession fees and cantonal taxes that could be executed in a transparent and verifiable way, reducing administrative times that are still partially manual or paper-based today.
So far the project is limited to a controlled protected environment. No public decision has been made on commercial launch to the general public; technical aspects (scalability, latency), operational aspects (compatibility with existing systems) and regulatory aspects (SNB regulations, FINMA, data protection) will first need to be clarified with the intervention of federal and cantonal authorities.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### When will the digital franc arrive on the Swiss market?
The date of a potential commercial launch remains uncertain. Testing continues until the end of 2026. Once the experimental phase is completed, federal authorities, the SNB, and participants will need to: resolve remaining technical issues (blockchain scalability, transaction latency, security protocols); define the regulatory and normative framework (how the CHFD integrates with Swiss laws on currency, anti-money laundering, data protection, and financial stability); assess the impact on national monetary policy and the stability of the Swiss financial system; verify compatibility with existing payment and settlement systems (SIC, SWIFT, debit/credit cards, banking applications).
Only then will the Federal Council, Parliament, or regulatory authorities formally decide whether the CHFD will be available for Swiss companies and the general public.
### What to expect until the end of 2026?
Until the end of 2026, developments will mainly concern the financial sector and regulatory authorities. Swiss citizens will not be able to use the CHFD during the test — it is reserved for the 9 participating companies in a protected environment — but they will be able to follow the progress through official statements from the SNB, FINMA, national economic media, and participating banks.
### Switzerland's positioning in global monetary innovation
The digital franc experiment positions Switzerland at the forefront of global monetary innovation. Countries like Sweden (with the e-krona), the Eurozone (with the digital euro), and China (with the digital yuan) are testing or preparing central bank digital currencies. Switzerland, with its reputed stable, neutral, and technologically advanced financial system, is not falling behind in this global transformation.
The outcome of this experiment could significantly influence Switzerland's monetary, payment, and financial innovation strategies in the coming years. If the CHFD receives approval from the authorities, it could represent a structural change in the way Swiss citizens, companies, and public administrations pay, transfer money, and interact with the national financial system.
To stay updated on the developments of the digital franc and how this could affect your payment tools and personal savings management, monitor official statements from the SNB and FINMA. Discover how to best manage your investments and financial planning with [our financial calculator](nav:calculator).

On July 24, 2026, the United States adopted additional tariffs on imports from several countries, including Switzerland. The action is based on an investigation into the trade of goods produced through forced labor, conducted under Section 301 of the 1974 US Trade Act. For Swiss imports, the USA applies an additional variable tariff that can reach 12.5%; these amounts are added to the MFN (Most Favored Nation) tariffs already in force, increasing the overall cost of access to the American market.
A few days after this announcement, on August 20, 2026, negotiations on the optimization of the free trade agreement between Switzerland and the United States concluded successfully. This development represents a significant sign of continuity in bilateral commercial dialogue, even in a context characterized by global tariff tensions.
The State Secretariat for the Economy (SECO) is the federal body responsible for managing international economic relations and supporting Swiss companies in scenarios of commercial change. The additional tariffs adopted on July 24 represent an immediate pressure on the competitiveness of Swiss companies oriented towards exports to the United States. A variable tariff up to 12.5%, applied on top of existing MFN tariffs, creates an increase in costs that enterprises must face. In a context of global competition, this over-taxation carries the risk of losing market share to competitors from other countries with more favorable tariff regimes. Profit margins narrow, or costs are transferred to U.S. customers, with potentially negative effects on demand.
### The counterbalance of the free trade agreement
The conclusion of negotiations for the optimization of the free trade agreement, communicated on August 20, 2026, introduces elements of strategic compensation. Although the source does not specify the technical details of the optimized agreement, the positive conclusion of the negotiations signals that the parties have found a balance between the tariff tensions arising from Section 301 and market access opportunities. This development partially balances the negative effect of tariffs, creating a more complex scenario in which risks and opportunities coexist.
### Scenarios for exporting companies
A Swiss company exporting to the USA faces a two-sided dynamic. On one hand, tariffs increase access costs to the American market up to an additional 12.5%. On the other hand, the optimized agreement could reduce trade barriers in other sectors of interest for Swiss exports or improve access conditions in specific areas. Enterprises must assess whether the goods they export fall within the categories affected by the Section 301 investigation (goods produced with forced labor) and whether they benefit from the new conditions of the agreement.

item.title: Your rent doesn't go down on its own. You have to ask for it
item.description: Mortgage rate stuck at 1.25%, but only 12% of tenants asked for a reduction. Here's how to check if you are entitled to pay less.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Mortgage rate stuck at 1.25% from September 2025 - Only 12% of tenants requested the second adjustment - Tenants must submit a written request to obtain the reduction - If the rent is at higher rates, the right to the reduction remains
## Key facts - **What**: Adjustment of the rent based on the reference mortgage rate - When: Rate stuck at 1.25% from 2 September 2025; confirmed to 2 September 2026 - Where: Switzerland (FOB - Federal Housing Office) - Who: Tenants and owners; Swiss Tenants Association - Percentage affected: Only 12% of tenants requested the second adjustment (April 2026) - Previous rates: 1.75% (before 2025), then 1.50%, currently 1.25%
The Swiss benchmark mortgage rate has remained stable at 1.25% since 2 September 2025. In September 2026, the Federal Housing Office (FOB) confirmed that the rate remains unchanged. However, this stability does not automatically mean that those who pay rent based on a higher rate can remain passive: if their rent is still calculated at 1.50% or higher, the right to a reduction remains intact.
The mechanism that regulates renter adjustments is simple but often ignored: the reduction in the rate does not automatically reduce the monthly rent. When rates rise, the owner or management communicates it directly to the tenant. When they come down, however, silence is the norm. The tenant must independently verify the situation and submit a formal written request to obtain the adjustment. [Se vuoi capire meglio come il costo della vita e l'alloggio influiscono sulle tue finanze personali, scopri di più nel nostro approfondimento](nav:cost-of-living).
In 2025, the mortgage rate dropped twice: first drop from 1.75% to 1.50%, second drop to 1.25%. Yet, according to data from the Zurich Cantonal Bank cited by the Swiss Tenants Association, in April 2026 only 12% of tenants had formally requested the second reduction. This meant that thousands of people continued to pay more rent than was justified by the current rate.
### What happened in September 2026
The UFAB communication of 2 September 2026 does not introduce a new decrease: the rate remains at 1.25%. However, the federal office explicitly states that the right to a reduction is still valid for those who have not yet formally acted. If you are paying rent at a rate higher than 1.25%, you can still request the adjustment retroactively. It is not too late, and the right does not expire. ### Because the reduction is not automatic
Here lies the heart of the problem. Rental contracts in Switzerland are governed by federal law (Code of Obligations), but do not provide for an automatic downward adjustment mechanism. When the owner increases the rent due to higher mortgage rates, communication is mandatory and occurs via formal notification. When rates drop, however, it is the tenant who has to take the initiative and submit the application.
The tenant must take the first step: check their contract, compare the declared rate with the UFAB's current reference mortgage rate, and submit a formal written request to the owner or management. A specific form is not required by law, but it is advisable to use a documented and certified form. TiAffitto, the model mentioned in the original source, is one of the standardized models available to facilitate the request.
### The numbers say it all
The 12% figure is eloquent and worrying at the same time. As of April 2026, almost nine out of ten tenants had not yet requested the second adjustment for 2025. This means that tens of thousands of people in Switzerland continued to pay a higher rent than justified by the reference rate. Many probably didn't even know they had the right to ask. Others knew but had put it off, didn't know how to proceed, or didn't fully understand the procedure.
If you are among them, it is never too late to act. As long as the reference rate remains at 1.25% and your rent is still calculated at a higher percentage, you have the legal right to ask for a reduction. The reduction can be recognized even months after the change in the official rate, without it being necessary to request immediately. There is no hard legal deadline to apply, although it is always advisable to act as soon as possible to start saving. Estimate the potential impact on your housing and economic situation using our analysis tools.
### How much you can save
The savings calculations depend on the amount of the monthly rent and the gap between the rate on which it is currently calculated and the reference rate of 1.25%. It is not a negligible amount for the family budget. On a rent of CHF 1,500 per month, every 0.25% difference in mortgage rate can mean a monthly saving of CHF 30–50. On an annual basis, this translates to CHF 360–600 that you are not claiming simply because you have not submitted the formal request to the owner.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to proceed: step-by-step
Step 1: Check your contract. Open the rental agreement and look for the clause that specifies the 'reference mortgage rate' or simply 'mortgage rate'. Note the exact percentage rate at which the rent is tied. If it is not specifically stated in the contract, contact the owner or management in writing and ask for it explicitly.
Step 2: Compare with the current rate. The UFAB reference rate from 2 September 2025 is 1.25%. If your contract says 1.50%, 1.75% or any other higher percentage, you have the right to request an adjustment of the rent to the current rate.
Step 3: Contact the owner or management. Send a registered letter (or certified email if accepted) formally requesting the adjustment of the rent to the current rate. Use a clear and precise formula: 'I request the rent adjustment based on the reference mortgage rate currently at 1.25%, as communicated by the UFAB on 2 September 2025'.
**Step 4: Keep your documentation.** Keep a copy of your request and any response you receive. If the owner refuses without reasons justified by law, you can appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority for rental disputes. The appeal is usually free or low cost.
### Where to find help
The Swiss Tenants Association has standardized forms (such as the aforementioned TiAffitto) and detailed guidelines to facilitate the request. Many cantons have specialized conciliation offices for tenancy disputes. In case of difficulties or unjustified refusals from the owner, you can contact a lawyer specialized in rental law, even if the first step—the letter of request—is simple and you can do it independently.
### Deadlines and rights
There is no legal 'deadline' for requesting rent reduction retroactively, but it is important to act as soon as possible. Federal law allows you to request an adjustment whenever the reference rate changes significantly. The recognition of the reduction normally begins from the month following the formal request, not from the month in which the rate officially changed. item.title: Family reunification: bureaucracy blocks children for years
item.description: A report by the Swiss Observatory denounces: slow procedures and difficult documents separate families up to the age of 10. Children pay the highest price.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Administrative procedures, not laws, are blocking family reunifications in Switzerland - Families examined remained separated for 9 to 10 years - Family reunifications in documented cases lasted up to 7 years - The Swiss Observatory demands a maximum duration of 1 year
## Key Facts - **Source**: Swiss Observatory for Asylum and Foreign Law (SBAA) - Publication: Report published Tuesday - Average separation duration: Between 9 and 10 years in examined cases - Family reunification procedure duration: Up to 7 years - SBAA Proposal: Maximum 1 year for application review - Main impact: On children and minors
It is not the laws that are blocking family reunifications in Switzerland, but rather the slowness of administrative procedures. This is the claim made on Tuesday by the Swiss Observatory for Asylum and Foreign Law (SBAA) with a new specialist report that particularly points to the devastating consequences for children.
The problems are concrete: documents that are difficult to obtain, high costs, and constant shifts of jurisdiction between federal and cantonal authorities. These obstacles, apparently technical, transform into years of family separation. In the cases examined by the report, families remained separated for nine to ten years.
### Administrative Obstacles
The main issue is obtaining the documents required by the authorities. In a specific case documented in the report, the authorities asked an Afghan man for an officially authenticated marriage certificate. To obtain it, the man was forced to return in person to Afghanistan, despite being in a dangerous situation. In another case involving a family of Eritrean refugees, an authority imposed the presentation of passports. To obtain them, the family members would have had to contact the authorities of the State from which they had fled, potentially putting their refugee status at risk. Only after a legal battle lasting two years was it recognized that this request was unacceptable.
Moreover, the procedures change depending on the competent authority. According to the report, the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) applies less strict criteria than cantonal authorities. This difference becomes problematic when jurisdiction shifts: if a person obtains a residence permit, the file is transferred from the Confederation to the Canton and the application is re-examined with more stringent requirements.
### Real Waiting Times
The family reunification procedures documented in the report lasted up to seven years. If you add the preceding asylum procedures and the waiting times provided by law, the separation can reach up to ten years: a substantial part of childhood that minors often spend abroad in precarious conditions and without secure residential status. ## The devastating impact on children
It is precisely children who suffer the most from procedural obstacles, the SBAA denounces in its report. During the years of waiting, minors find themselves separated from their parents in often precarious conditions, without legal certainty regarding their future in the country. The time of separation coincides with crucial years of their growth and development.
The situation worsens further when the dossiers pass from the federal to the cantonal authorities. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) applies different procedural standards than the cantons, and this creates a cascade effect: when responsibility passes from the Confederation to the canton, the dossier is subjected to a new examination with more stringent requirements. As a result, families who had gone through procedures at the SEM find themselves forced to start the process practically from scratch at the cantonal office.
### The requests of the Swiss Observatory
Faced with this situation, the Swiss Observatory for the Right to Asylum and Foreigners has made concrete requests to the federal and cantonal authorities. The main proposal is to set the maximum duration for examining family reunification applications at one year, a term currently absent from the regulations.
In addition to the time limit, the SBAA requests that the authorities consistently take into account the special protection needs, especially of minors. This means not only speeding up times, but also adapting procedures to the vulnerable conditions of children. Finally, the report emphasizes that testing requirements should be tailored to the conditions of the country of origin and the protection status of the persons involved, avoiding imposing requirements that put the safety of applicants at risk.
Currently, requests for documents such as notarized certificates, passports or other official documents remain a major obstacle, especially when documentation needs to be obtained from states from which people have had to flee due to persecution.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## How the reunification process works
Family reunification in Switzerland is a process that involves both federal and cantonal responsibilities. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) is the federal body that manages the first stages, but the dossier can pass to the cantonal authorities once the applicant obtains a residence permit. This transfer of competence, formally necessary for the Swiss administration, represents one of the critical points highlighted by the report.
Anyone who is in a situation of family separation and has well-founded reasons for reunification must prepare documentation demonstrating the family bond and the reasons why reunification is necessary. The documents required vary, but often include marriage certificates, birth certificates, and other documents that should be officially notarized. As emerges from the Observatory's report, this very phase of document collection is often the one that takes the longest, especially when the people involved come from countries where obtaining official certificates is complicated or dangerous.
### What to do if you find yourself in this situation
If you are facing a family separation and considering submitting a reunification application, it is essential to carefully document all your communications with the authorities and response times. Keep copies of every document sent and every response received from the SEM or the competent cantonal authority.
Contact the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) to understand which documents are specifically required in your case. When doing so, clearly indicate whether there are legitimate impediments to obtaining documents from certain countries. If your application is transferred to the cantonal authority, immediately check what additional requirements the canton may impose and ask for clarification to avoid further delays.
Consider [consultare gli annunci di lavoro in Svizzera](nav:jobs) if you are planning a long-term move, as a stable employment situation can ease administrative processes. Furthermore, [informarvi sul costo della vita nel Paese](nav:cost-of-living) will help you financially plan family reunification once the administrative procedures have been completed.

item.title: Novartis: setback in the neuromuscular sector
item.description: Novartis fails the Harbor study for the drug del-désiran in myotonic dystrophy type 1. It is the second negative trial in a few days, but the company maintains a 5-6% annual growth target for 2025-2030.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Novartis fails Harbor trial for del-désiran drug on type 1 myotonic dystrophy - Does not achieve primary objective despite "signs of clinical efficacy" - It is the second clinical failure in a few days for the Basel giant - Growth target of 5-6% per year 2025-2030 remains confirmed
## Key facts - **What**: Failure of the Harbor clinical trial - Drug tested: delpacibart etédésiran (del-désiran) - Therapeutic indication: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) - Outcome: Primary objective not achieved - Sequence: Second trial failure in a few days - Corporate headquarters: Basel, Switzerland - Economic prospects: Annual growth 5-6% confirmed 2025-2030
The multinational pharmaceutical company Novartis, based in Basel, has announced the failure of the clinical trial called "Harbor", dedicated to the drug delpacibart etédésiran (del-désiran) for the treatment of myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1). According to the company's official statement, the study did not meet its primary objective, although it demonstrated detectable "signals of clinical efficacy" during development.
This setback represents the second major late-stage clinical trial failure announced by Novartis in a matter of days. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is a degenerative genetic disease of the neuromuscular system, and the tested drug represented a possible therapeutic path for patients suffering from this rare disease.
### The meaning of clinical failure
Not reaching the primary objective of a clinical trial is a disappointing outcome from a scientific and strategic perspective, but it is an intrinsic part of the pharmaceutical development process. Novartis has invested years and significant resources researching del-désiran for the neuromuscular indication, and this announcement marks a major milestone in the development program.
However, it is crucial to understand that “signals of clinical efficacy” observed during the study are not sufficient to proceed towards regulatory approval. International regulatory bodies, including the Swiss agency Swissmedic, require that the drug clearly achieves the primary endpoints before the formal review phase.
### Confidence confirmed despite obstacles
Despite recent clinical failures in the neuromuscular sector, Novartis has maintained full confidence in its overall economic prospects. The company confirmed its annual growth target of between 5% and 6% for the period 2025-2030. This signal is relevant for Swiss stakeholders: the multinational recognizes the obstacles in research, but considers its commercial strategy solid.
Confirmation of the growth target remains an indicator of Novartis' portfolio diversification. With dozens of therapeutic programs in development in different areas, failure to achieve the objective of the Harbor study does not compromise the company's expected consolidated performance in the coming years. ### Implications for the Swiss research economy
Novartis represents one of the pillars of the Swiss pharmaceutical industry and the overall national economy. Headquartered in Basel, it employs tens of thousands of people in Switzerland and maintains a comprehensive network of research, development and manufacturing facilities. Clinical trial failures, although they do not cause immediate dramatic economic effects, influence the company's market valuation, institutional investor confidence and sentiment in the Swiss life sciences sector.
Novartis' neuromuscular research strategy was a recognized priority. The drug del-désiran had been identified as a promising drug candidate for a rare and severe disease. Failure to achieve the primary endpoint in the Harbor study means that the regulatory path to approval for this therapeutic indication has been interrupted, at least temporarily, requiring a strategic reevaluation of the program.
However, it is important to highlight that Novartis operates on a very large and diverse portfolio of research projects. A single clinical failure, while significant from a scientific and commercial perspective, does not compromise the overall strength of the company's business model or Novartis' position in the global pharmaceutical market.
### Switzerland's role as a clinical research hub
Switzerland is a recognized international hub for the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industry. Novartis, together with other large players such as Roche and GSK, represents the strategic core of this industry. Massive investments in research and development, including complex clinical trials such as Harbor, keep the Swiss economy competitive and attractive in the global life sciences and sciences sector.
Announcements such as the failure of the Harbor study have implications that ripple across Swiss industry: university and hospital researchers collaborating with multinational pharmaceutical companies, diagnostic and clinical service providers, specialized research institutes, and patient organizations. Excellent research in this area requires constant investment, acceptance of scientific risk and a deep-rooted culture of innovation.
### Growth prospects and diversification strategy
Despite the failure of the Harbor study, Novartis maintains its annual growth target of 5-6% for 2025-2030. This goal reflects a deliberate diversification strategy: the company's overall success does not depend on a single therapeutic program, but on the sum of numerous research initiatives in different fields, expected regulatory approvals, penetration into emerging markets and operational efficiency.
The confirmation of the growth target is a message that international market analysts will monitor carefully. If Novartis can maintain this growth trajectory despite recent clinical failures in the neuromuscular space, it will demonstrate the resilience of the business model and the validity of the diversified portfolio strategy domestically and globally.

Anyone interested in the performance of Novartis and the Swiss pharmaceutical sector should follow several strategic indicators. The company's official communications on clinical trial results are published through Novartis' official channels and represent the primary source of information. Investors can monitor the performance of the stock on international exchanges, while industry professionals follow announcements on new therapeutic programs, expected regulatory approvals and strategic partnerships.
The international clinical trial registration portal ClinicalTrials.gov provides public, up-to-date information on studies like Harbor, clinical research progress, research sites and inclusion criteria. This tool is valuable both for patients suffering from rare diseases such as myotonic dystrophy type 1 who are looking for opportunities to access experimental drugs, and for professionals and investors who wish to monitor the scientific panorama of Swiss and international pharmaceutical research.
Novartis regularly publishes detailed quarterly reports and annual financial statements with data on economic performance, status of the pipeline of drugs in development, results of significant clinical trials and strategic adjustments. For those who live and work in Switzerland and have a personal, professional or investment interest in the healthcare and biotechnology sector, these documents provide concrete and verifiable information.
### Access to experimental drugs and the Swiss healthcare system
The failure of the Harbor study also illustrates the importance of excellent clinical research conducted in Switzerland. Swiss hospital centers and accredited research institutes regularly participate in international clinical trials of multinational pharmaceutical companies, contributing with expertise and patient recruitment sites to studies such as Harbor.
For patients with rare diseases such as myotonic dystrophy type 1, participation in controlled clinical trials can represent an opportunity to access experimental therapies when approved therapeutic options are unavailable or insufficient. The Swiss healthcare system, regulated by KVG law (mandatory health insurance), includes specific mechanisms for access to experimental drugs through compassionate use programs and extended access in particular clinical situations, always subject to rigorous ethical evaluation.
### Tools and resources for investors and professionals
Those who own Novartis shares or consider investing in the Swiss pharmaceutical sector should consult an independent financial advisor to evaluate how clinical failures of specific programs impact their personal investment strategy. Despite the confirmed growth target for 2025-2030, every investment involves risk and diversification remains a fundamental principle of risk management.

item.title: Updated UN sanctions: SESAM amended on 7 September
item.description: The UN committee amended the sanctions lists on 7 September 2026. The SESAM database automatically updates the restrictive measures in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Update of UN sanctions lists on 7 September 2026 - SESAM database automatically updated in Switzerland - Immediate validity by federal ordinance of 4 March 2016 - Banks and businesses must verify compliance
## Key facts - **What**: Changes to the UN sanctions list (persons, companies, organizations) - When: 7 September 2026 - Where: Bern (Swiss federal coordination) - Who: UN Sanctions Committee and Federal Council - Validity: Immediate in Switzerland via ordinance
Bern, 7 September 2026. The United Nations Sanctions Committee has modified the list of individuals, companies and organizations subject to sanctions. The SESAM database, the Swiss central international compliance system, has been updated accordingly. According to the official communication from the Federal Administration, the changes acquire immediate legal validity in Swiss territory.
The underlying mechanism dates back to 4 March 2016, when the Federal Council approved a decisive ordinance: the automatic transposition of the United Nations Security Council sanctions lists. This rule eliminates bureaucratic delays between the UN decision and implementation in Switzerland. No new federal decrees, parliamentary ratifications or further administrative steps are needed. The change to the UN list comes into force instantly, binding economic operators and financial institutions to comply.
### How SESAM transfigures sanctions into legal obligation
The SESAM database represents the bridge between the UN resolutions and the Swiss legal system. When the sanctions committee modifies a list — adding or removing people, companies or organizations — the modification is immediately reported in SESAM and becomes binding on anyone operating in Switzerland. Banks, asset management companies, foreign trade companies and economic operators in general must verify customers and suppliers against the updated UN lists. On September 7, 2026, this verification became even more critical: the list has changed and any financial institution that does not update its controls risks serious violations. ### Automatic transposition and practical implications
The Federal Council's decision of 4 March 2016 represents a paradigm shift in the management of sanctions in Switzerland. Rather than wait for Parliament to legislate on each new UN measure, the Swiss government decided to delegate the power to update the lists directly to the UN Security Council. This approach reflects Switzerland's commitment to the multilateral system and to the fight against the financing of terrorism and illicit activities.
The operational consequence is immediate: no Swiss bank, no commercial company, no economic operator can claim not to be aware of a UN sanction. The September 7, 2026 amendment is effective as of September 7, 2026. Anyone who continues to transact with a sanctioned entity after that date commits a serious violation and becomes liable to administrative and criminal sanctions.
Each credit institution must implement automatic screening systems that compare its customers and suppliers against the updated SESAM database. The checks must take place: (1) at the time the commercial relationship is established; (2) periodically (at least monthly or quarterly); (3) immediately, as soon as a change is made public. A passive periodic check is not enough. Compliance requires active diligence and documentation of audits.
### What changes in the scope of sanctions
The UN list includes individuals, groups, businesses and international organizations believed to be linked to threats to international peace and security, terrorism, or weapons proliferation. The September 7, 2026 update changed this perimeter — although the official communication does not specify exactly which entities have been added or removed, every Swiss operator must assume that at least one change has occurred and act accordingly.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Concrete procedures: how to verify compliance
Economic operators and financial institutions must perform three levels of control. First level: initial verification when opening an account, establishing a business relationship or signing a contract. The new customer must be checked against SESAM before any transaction takes place. Second level: recurring periodic control. Most Swiss banks implement automatic monthly or quarterly screening. Third level: immediate reporting and blocking. If a match emerges, the bank must immediately freeze the funds, warn the customer (in certain cases) and report to the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) and the enforcement authorities.
Documentation of these checks is mandatory. Swiss supervisory authorities regularly inspect credit institutions to ensure compliance with compliance checks. A gap in verification — or blatant negligence — exposes the institution to significant administrative fines and, in extreme cases, to criminal prosecution for money laundering or violations of economic sanctions.
### Where to find SESAM and updates
The SESAM database is managed by the Swiss Federal Administration and publicly accessible online. Economic operators, legal consultants, financial sector professionals and banks connect directly to the portal to download and consult the updated lists. Each change, such as that of September 7, 2026, is made available in real time.
Furthermore, the Federal Council and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs issue official communications when important changes occur. Businesses that engage in international trade, manage foreign funds or have foreign clients must subscribe to automatic notifications from SESAM to be notified immediately of updates.
**Recommended Action**: Check your business's compliance with the updated SESAM list now. If you manage commercial relationships or accounts with entities of foreign origin, rely on consultants specialized in international compliance for an in-depth check.

item.title: Rösti promises compensation for waste storage
item.description: Rösti presents the project for the Lägern Nord depot between Zurich and Aargau in Fisibach. Promised compensations, decision towards 2030, storage from 2050.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Rösti presents the Lägern Nord depot in Fisibach, over 400 people present - Deep deposit between AG and ZH in opaline clay, hundreds of meters deep - Promised compensation; CF decision ~2030, voting ~2030, storage by 2050
- **What**: Deep repository for radioactive waste (Lägern Nord) - When: CF decision ~2030, voting ~2030, storage from 2050 - Where: Lägern Nord (north-west Bülach), between cantons Zurich and Aargau - Who: Federal Councilor Albert Rösti (DETEC), Nagra, over 400 participants - Document: Nagra applied November 2024
### The Fisibach event
Albert Rösti, federal councilor and head of DETEC, appeared in Fisibach (Aargau) to illustrate the project for a deep repository for the safe storage of Swiss radioactive waste in front of over 400 people. The structure should be built in the Lägern Nord area, between the cantons of Zurich and Aargau.
During the meeting, Rösti assured the population of a "transparent, progressive and jointly conducted" approach and announced compensation for the region. He stressed that the safe disposal of radioactive waste is a national responsibility that cannot be delegated to future generations, with safety as the top priority. He also thanked the local population for taking on "an important project for the whole of Switzerland".
### The decision-making process towards 2050
The institutional path is complex and extends over several decades. The Federal Council should decide on the final choice of the site around 2030, considering the various objections received during the consultative phase. Subsequently, it will be up to Parliament to give its approval to the project.
Swiss direct democracy will have a crucial say: Rösti expects a popular vote around 2030. If approved by the people, the storage of the first radioactive waste should begin in 2050. This means that the project, although decided in the next few years, will not enter the operational phase for at least two decades. ### The Lägern Nord site: geology and precise location
The depot is planned to the north-west of Bülach, in the canton of Zurich, in a strategic position between the two cantons involved. The structure will descend hundreds of meters deep within a geological layer of opaline clay, chosen for its natural insulation properties and long-term stability.
The main access to the complex will be located in Stadel, canton of Zurich. However, the waste treatment facilities will not be built directly at the deep repository, but at the already existing intermediate repository in Würenlingen, Aargau. This geographical separation between the access location, the processing space and the deep storage reflects an optimization of logistics and safety processes dictated by national technical needs.
### Nagra and the federal administrative process
Responsibility for the entire project falls on the Cooperative Society for the Storage of Radioactive Waste (Nagra). In November 2024, Nagra submitted the official application for the construction of the depot to the Confederation, marking the formal start of the technical, administrative and political evaluation by the federal authorities.
Nagra's application represents the fruit of years of geological research and technical evaluations, culminating in the proposal for a site that combines safety requirements, geological stability and logistical feasibility. Approval by the Confederation (expected around 2030) will not be a formality: the Federal Council will have to assess the technical suitability of the site, the adequacy of the safety plans and the response to the objections raised by local communities and cantonal bodies.
### Next steps and the role of the population
The path to 2050 will be long and will require continuous dialogue between Nagra, the federal and cantonal authorities, and the interested population. Rösti confirmed that the process will be "conducted together with the population", indicating that local consultations will not be merely formal. Communities in Fisibach, Stadel, Würenlingen and surrounding areas will have the opportunity to express concerns during the federal consultation phases.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### The promised compensations: what will be defined
Rösti has announced compensation for the region affected by the project, but details regarding the amount, how it will be distributed and the specific beneficiaries have not yet been made public. This is a crucial issue for local communities: the presence of a national infrastructure of this kind brings national benefits but also territorial impacts such as land occupation, prolonged construction activities and long-term monitoring.
The compensations represent a recognition of this disparity: the Confederation recognizes that the cantons and municipalities concerned (Aargau and Zurich) support a project of national interest that does not generate immediate local economic benefits. Details on the composition, size and distribution of compensation will need to be negotiated and defined in the years leading up to the federal decision around 2030.
One of Rösti's key commitments was to emphasize the role of local people in decision-making. It guaranteed a "transparent, progressive and conducted together with the population" approach. This means that affected communities will not simply be informed ex post, but will have the opportunity to express concerns, criticisms and proposals during the consultative phases.
In Switzerland, federal decisions of this magnitude follow a principle of direct democracy involving both Parliament and citizens. The popular vote towards 2030 will be the crucial moment in which all Swiss will be able to express their opinion, not just residents of the affected cantons. This opens up broader debates on national responsibility for the nuclear waste cycle and on the fair sharing of infrastructure burdens.
### What to monitor in the coming years
Residents and cantonal authorities will need to remain active in the years leading up to 2030. The federal consultative process will seek feedback on safety, environmental, infrastructure and compensatory issues. The cantonal administrations of Zurich and Aargau will play a decisive role in collecting and transmitting the concerns of their citizens to the federal authorities.
Rösti's decision to visit Fisibach and promise compensation signals a recognition by the Confederation that local debate is legitimate and important for the overall success of the project. The next few years will be decisive in defining the exact contours of the deposit and its territorial implications.

item.title: IVF in Switzerland: Costs are not covered
item.description: In vitro fertilization costs up to 8,000 francs and is not reimbursed by KVG. One expert calls it "an injustice" because the WHO recognizes infertility as a disease.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - IVF costs up to 8'000 CHF and is not reimbursed by basic insurance - 50% of patients do not need IVF to conceive naturally - WHO recognizes infertility as a disease, but Switzerland does not cover it
## Key facts - **What**: In vitro fertilization not covered by KVG in Switzerland - Who: Fabien Murisier, director of the Medically Assisted Procreation Center (CPMA), Lausanne - Where: Lausanne and Switzerland - Amount: CHF 8'000 first cycle CHF 500-1'500 drugs - Percentage of patients without need for IVF: 50% - Statistics: Approximately 6,500 couples/year resort to reproductive medicine - Establishment: WHO recognizes infertility as a disease
In vitro fertilization is often the last option for those who are unable to have children naturally. In Switzerland, although infertility is recognized internationally as a disease, resorting to IVF involves an initial cost of around 8,000 francs. A cost that falls entirely on the patient's shoulders, without any guarantee of pregnancy and without reimbursement from basic insurance.
«An injustice», according to Fabien Murisier, director of the Center for Medically Assisted Procreation (CPMA) in Lausanne. "Reimbursing also means recognizing illness and suffering," underlined the expert.
### The path is partially covered
Every year in Switzerland around 6,500 couples turn to reproductive medicine. Yet not everyone necessarily needs to resort to in vitro fertilization. «Almost 50% of our patients manage to have a child without going through IVF», explains Murisier.
The healthcare system covers part of the reproductive path. Tests to understand the causes of infertility are reimbursed, as are some treatments: stimulation of ovulation for one year or up to three attempts at intrauterine insemination. For the other half of the patients, who must resort to IVF, the costs are entirely at their own expense. [Scopri la copertura LAMal per la medicina della riproduzione](nav:health).
### The real numbers of IVF
A first IVF costs around 8,000 francs, to which must be added between 500 and 1,500 francs for the necessary drugs. Failure does not mean having to start from scratch: IVF often allows you to obtain several embryos, and those not transferred immediately can be frozen for subsequent attempts. Each new transfer costs around 2,000 francs.
If the patient no longer has frozen embryos, she must repeat the entire procedure with all the associated costs. The final bill can vary greatly from one patient to the next, making it impossible to establish an average amount spent until the birth of a child. The WHO recognizes infertility as a disease, yet in Switzerland it remains completely the responsibility of the patient. ### Financial injustice and cultural taboo
It is precisely the variability of costs that makes the situation financially unfair. As Murisier points out, it is impossible to establish an average price for the complete journey up to birth. The mother's age has a huge impact on the outcome: the older she gets, the fewer embryos are obtained and the greater the risk of chromosomal anomalies. Some patients will get pregnant on the first transfer, others will need three or four attempts. This unpredictability makes the situation financially unfair and creates unacceptable inequalities in the right to access parenting.
In addition to the economic issue, the reimbursement would have an important symbolic value. Infertility remains surrounded by a certain cultural taboo in Switzerland, with the idea sometimes implied that the people affected are responsible for their own situation: too stressed or that it is enough to "leave it to nature". “The same would not be said for other diseases, such as cancer, for example,” underlines Murisier. Recognition through reimbursement would also mean dispelling this taboo and openly addressing the issue of infertility.
### The unequal treatment between heterosexual couples and female couples
There is a further difference in treatment in the Swiss healthcare system. If for a heterosexual couple with infertility problems some treatments are partially covered, for a couple made up of two women the situation is different. Health insurance companies generally believe that it is not infertility caused by illness and refuse to cover insemination with donor sperm.
«The vast majority of female couples we follow do not need IVF. In approximately 95% of cases we proceed with inseminations", specifies Murisier. Yet, precisely because those couples are not considered to be suffering from medical infertility, they remain without insurance coverage, creating a clear disparity in rights and access. 📊 This distinction reveals the inconsistency of the system: if infertility is a disease recognized by the WHO, the path to achieving a pregnancy — regardless of sexual orientation — should be treated the same way from an insurance point of view.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Where and how to contact
For those who live in Switzerland and find themselves in a situation of infertility, the first step is to consult your GP or a gynecologist for an evaluation. Diagnostic tests to identify the causes are generally covered by basic insurance, as are the first year of ovarian stimulation or up to three attempts at intrauterine insemination.
If these treatments do not bring results and the doctor believes that IVF is necessary, it is essential to be aware that the costs will not be covered. It is therefore necessary:
- Contact specialized facilities such as medically assisted procreation centers (CPMA) to obtain a realistic estimate of costs for your specific case - Contact your health insurance company to see which items may be partially covered - Check whether your KVG policy provides additional coverage which could include assisted reproduction
### Financial planning and options
According to Murisier and other experts, IVF reimbursement falls within the logic of inclusive healthcare that recognizes infertility as a disease and not as a personal choice. Although it is not currently covered by the Swiss basic insurance system, it is important to monitor political debates that could change this situation.
In the meantime, it is advisable to check whether some health insurance companies offer coverage for reproductive medicine. Each canton may also have specific guidelines for couples facing infertility issues. 💡 Disparities in costs and coverage make a personalized consultation with your insurance essential before embarking on an IVF process.
To better plan the financial implications and understand the various options available in your canton, compare the different Swiss health insurance companies and discover their coverage.

item.title: Meeting of social ministers in Luxembourg: focus on pensions and health
item.description: On 7 September 2026 in Luxembourg, Switzerland signed a declaration with Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein and Luxembourg on pensions, NCDs and neurodegenerative diseases.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 07.09.2026, Luxembourg - Meeting of the social ministers of the German-speaking countries - Signature of a joint declaration on pensions, NCDs, and neurodegeneration
## Key facts - **What**: Annual meeting on pension systems, non-communicable and neurodegenerative diseases - When: 07.09.2026 - Where: Luxembourg - Who: Ministers of social affairs and health from Switzerland, Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, and Luxembourg - Amount: Not yet specified
On September 7, 2026, in Luxembourg, the head of the Federal Department of Home Affairs participated in the annual meeting with their counterparts from Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, and Luxembourg. The agenda featured the modernization of pension systems, the prevention of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and the social consequences of neurodegenerative diseases. At the end of the meeting, a joint declaration was signed in which the five countries reaffirmed their commitment to continuing close cooperation.
### Meeting details Focus was placed on the long-term stability of pension systems, considered a fundamental challenge in light of demographic changes. The ministers highlighted the need to adapt social security not only to population aging but also to new life paths and emerging forms of work. In parallel, non-communicable diseases—cardiovascular, cancer, and mental illnesses—were identified as one of the major health challenges in Europe. The participants agreed on the importance of creating favorable conditions for health, integrating preventive measures into primary care, and reducing avoidable risk factors.
Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson's disease and dementia, were highlighted for their impact on both patients and health systems. The ministers discussed how to rapidly integrate the results of scientific research into clinical practice, focusing on innovative care models, prevention, and social participation. The final declaration centered on the future of pension systems, prevention, and health promotion, also referring to the risks associated with heatwaves. The next meeting is scheduled for 2027 in Liechtenstein.
To explore the tax and social security implications of these topics, please consult our [salary calculator](nav:calculator). ## Practical Analysis The Luxembourg meeting, while not containing immediate legislative decisions, anticipates possible developments that will directly affect Swiss taxpayers. The modernization of pension systems, which is at the center of the debate, could lead to adjustments in the calculation parameters of the AHV/AVS and the BVG/LPP, especially for workers with atypical career paths. A potential alignment with Austrian or German models could introduce new contribution brackets or modify the reference age thresholds.
### Implications for taxpayers - **AHV/AVS contributions**: currently, the employee's share is 5.3% (10.6% in total). A potential increase to support long-term stability would impact the monthly net salary of all earners, including cross-border commuters. - BVG/LPP: current rates vary from 7% to 18% depending on age. Any revision could increase the contribution burden, especially for employees over 45 years old. - NCD prevention: the emphasis on preventive measures could translate into tax incentives for workplace health programs, with possible deductions in the federal direct tax return.
Neurodegenerative diseases, cited as an emerging challenge, could push authorities to strengthen long-term care services, with possible repercussions on social security (AI/IV) contributions. Furthermore, the emphasis on heatwave periods suggests that cantonal health authorities might introduce environmental health monitoring programs, with indirect impacts on LAMal/KVG insurance costs.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Recommended Action Swiss citizens and workers should prepare for potential changes by monitoring official communications from the Federal Department of Home Affairs and their respective cantons. Here is a step-by-step guide to follow:
1. **Subscribe to newsletters** from your canton and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) to receive updates on pension reforms. 2. Check your contribution status on the AHV/IV portal: review the current rate (5.3% for employees) and compare your BVG balance. 3. Assess potential prevention incentives: some cantons offer discounts on health insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG) for corporate wellness programs; consult your insurer. 4. Plan your financial future using our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate scenarios involving contribution increases. 5. Participate in public consultations when the government launches pension system reform proposals; participation is often open to all residents. 6. Update your documentation: keep pay slips, health insurance certificates, and BVG contribution statements readily available.
